d: The deep ocean is not one place but a stack of very different worlds. A guide to the five depth zones, from the sunlit surface to the hadal trenches.
x: The ocean covers about 71% of Earth, but most of it is deep ocean , conventionally anything below 200 m. The deep ocean covers about 66% of the planet’s entire surface 3 . Oceanographers divide the water column into zones by how much sunlight reaches them. Light, more than anything else, controls where food is made and how animals live. Key facts Deep ocean begins where sunlight dwindles, at about 200 m 1 . Pressure rises by about 1 atmosphere every 10 m of seawater 2 , reaching about 1,100 atm in the deepest trench. Most of the ocean is 2,000–6,000 m deep , and most of that is cold (≈0–4 °C) and dark. The five pelagic zones # Zone Depth Light What defines it Epipelagic (sunlight) 0–200 m Enough for photosynthesis Phytoplankton make the food that feeds almost everything below Mesopelagic (twilight) 200–1,000 m Dim blue, fading to none The largest daily animal migration on Earth: lanternfish and krill rise at night to feed Bathypelagic (midnight) 1,000–4,000 m None from the Sun Light comes only from bioluminescence; food arrives as “marine snow” Abyssopelagic (abyss) 4,000–6,000 m None Near-freezing, very low food, vast flat abyssal plains Hadopelagic (hadal) 6,000–~11,000 m None Ocean trenches at subduction zones; extreme pressure and endemic species Why the boundaries matter # 200 m: the end of photosynthesis. Below this depth there isn’t enough light for net primary production. Every animal deeper down depends on food that sinks or migrates from above, or (at vents and seeps) on chemical energy from the Earth. That is why deep ecosystems are often food-limited, and why the twilight zone acts as a gatekeeper. It decides how much surface carbon gets exported to depth (see The biological carbon pump ). 1,000 m: total darkness. Below about a kilometre no sunlight is detectable, even to animals with extremely sensitive eyes. Vision shifts from seeing sunlight to seeing living light, and many species evolve red pigments that look black in blue-dominated light. 6,000 m: the hadal frontier. Trenches are isolated “islands” of extreme depth. Their faunas are distinctive, and they hold life’s depth records: fish to ~8,300 m, and chemosynthetic animal communities down to 9,533 m (see Hadal life ). Benthic zones: the seafloor equivalents # The seafloor has parallel names: bathyal (continental slope, ~200–4,000 m), abyssal (4,000–6,000 m) and hadal (6,000 m+). Most deep-sea biodiversity lives here, on or in the sediment, rather than in the open water. How we know so little # Even these “textbook” boundaries rest on remarkably few direct observations. A 2025 study estimated that only about 0.001% of the deep seafloor has ever been imaged 3 . See How little we have seen . d: The three physical gradients that shape all deep-sea life, with the physics behind each and what they mean for animals and machines.
x: Three physical gradients define the deep sea. Pressure climbs in a straight line, light collapses exponentially, and temperature drops sharply then flattens. Each one sets hard limits on biology and engineering. Pressure: linear and relentless # Seawater adds roughly one atmosphere of pressure for every ~10 m of depth 1 : P ≈ 1 atm + depth (m) / 10.06 At the abyssal plain (~4,500 m) that is ~450 atm. At the Challenger Deep (~10,935 m) it is about 1,090 atm, roughly 110 MPa , the weight of about a tonne pressing on every square centimetre. What pressure does to life. High pressure squeezes molecules. It changes how proteins fold, makes cell membranes stiff and slows enzymes. Deep-sea animals adapt in three main ways: Piezolytes , small molecules that stabilise proteins. The best known is TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide), whose concentration in fish muscle rises with depth 4 . Flexible membranes with more unsaturated fats, which stay fluid under pressure. No gas spaces. Deep fishes such as snailfish lack swim bladders, because gas would be compressed to almost nothing. Why fish stop at ~8,200–8,400 m. TMAO concentrations rise so much with depth that, extrapolated, fish tissue would become saltier (more concentrated) than seawater at roughly 8,200 m. That would cause osmotic problems. The deepest fish ever filmed, a snailfish at 8,336 m , sits right at this predicted limit 4 . Invertebrates face no identical ceiling, which is why tubeworms and amphipods live deeper. Light: exponential collapse # Sunlight is absorbed and scattered as it passes through water. Red goes first (within ~10 m), then yellow and green, and blue penetrates furthest. In very clear ocean water, roughly 1% of surface light remains near 100 m. Effectively no photosynthesis is possible below about 200 m 3 , and no sunlight is detectable below about 1,000 m. Consequences: Colour: red animals look black in the deep because there is no red light to reflect. Eyes: twilight-zone animals have huge or tubular eyes tuned to blue. Some deep fishes add red-light “searchlights” that most prey cannot see. Bioluminescence becomes the main light source. See Bioluminescence . Temperature: a thermocline, then cold stability # Surface water ranges from below 0 °C at the poles to ~30 °C in the tropics. Below the thermocline (typically within the upper ~1,000 m), temperatures drop to a remarkably uniform ~0–4 °C throughout most of the deep ocean 2 . Exceptions are hydrothermal vents, where fluids can exceed 350 °C, and the warm (~13 °C) deep Mediterranean. Cold slows metabolism. Combined with scarce food, it explains the slow life histories of many deep animals: slow growth, late maturity and long lifespans. Some deep-sea corals live for thousands of years. Slow life histories are also why deep ecosystems recover so slowly from damage (see Deep-sea mining ). Engineering at depth # Every vehicle that goes deep must handle the same pressure. Full-ocean-depth crew spheres use thick titanium hulls. Buoyancy comes from syntactic foam (glass microspheres in resin), because air-filled floats would be crushed. Electronics are either pressure-housed or oil-filled and pressure-compensated. See Vehicles and technology . Try it yourself # The Dive Profile Lab lets you drag a probe from 0 to 10,935 m and watch pressure, light, temperature, a balloon’s volume (Boyle’s law) and the resident life change. d: How cold, salty water sinks at the poles and slowly ventilates the entire deep ocean, and why the AMOC is the conveyor's most watched link.
x: The deep ocean is not stagnant. Water that sinks in a few polar regions spreads along the seafloor across entire basins, rises slowly, and eventually returns to the surface. One full loop takes on the order of a thousand years . This thermohaline circulation (driven by temperature, “thermo”, and salinity, “haline”) carries oxygen into the deep, stores heat and carbon, and shapes climate. How water sinks # Seawater gets denser when it gets colder or saltier . In winter, two regions make water dense enough to sink to the abyss: North Atlantic (Nordic, Labrador and Irminger seas): strong cooling makes North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) , which flows south at ~1,500–4,000 m. Around Antarctica : sea-ice formation rejects salt into very cold water, forming Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) , the densest water in the ocean. It hugs the seafloor and spreads north into every basin. That sinking water carries dissolved oxygen taken up at the surface. It is why most of the deep ocean is oxygenated at all. Where ventilation is weak, oxygen minimum zones form (see Deoxygenation ). The AMOC # The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is the Atlantic part of this system. Warm surface water (including the Gulf Stream) flows north, releases heat to the atmosphere (keeping north-western Europe mild), cools, sinks, and returns south at depth. Measured and projected Observations from arrays at four latitudes show the AMOC weakening over the past two decades (University of Miami study, April 2026) 1 . An observation-constrained projection finds 43–59% weakening by 2100 . That is about 60% stronger than the average climate model 2 . Full analysis: Portmann et al. 2026 . Why the deep ocean cares # Oxygen supply. Less sinking means less oxygen delivered to the deep North Atlantic. Heat and carbon storage. The overturning pushes heat and anthropogenic CO₂ into the interior. Changes alter where and how much is stored. Larval connectivity. Deep currents carry the larvae of vent, seep and coral species between isolated habitats. Upwelling: the return path # Deep water returns to the surface mainly in the Southern Ocean , where westerly winds draw it up along sloping density surfaces, and through slow mixing elsewhere. Coastal upwelling (Peru, California, Benguela) brings nutrient-rich water up and fuels some of the world’s richest fisheries. Beneath these productive zones lie some of the largest oxygen minimum zones. Open questions # How close is the AMOC to a tipping point? Some studies argue collapse may already be committed 3 . The IPCC’s AR6 assessment still calls collapse before 2100 “very unlikely” (medium confidence). How will Antarctic Bottom Water formation respond to Antarctic meltwater? Several studies report it slowing. See the full climate treatment in AMOC weakening . d: How marine snow, migrating animals and seafloor sediments move carbon from the surface into the deep ocean for centuries to millennia, and what threatens that service.
x: The ocean holds far more carbon than the atmosphere, land plants and soils combined 1 . It has absorbed roughly a quarter of the CO₂ humans emitted between the early 1960s and late 2010s 2 . Part of that uptake is physical: CO₂ dissolves in cold water that then sinks. Part is biological , through the biological carbon pump . How the pump works # Fixation. Phytoplankton in the sunlit zone turn CO₂ into organic carbon by photosynthesis. Export. A fraction sinks as marine snow : dead plankton, faecal pellets and mucus aggregates falling through the twilight zone. Attenuation. Most of that snow is eaten or decomposed by microbes in the upper ~1,000 m, releasing CO₂ back into the water at depth. Sequestration. Carbon that reaches the deep ocean stays out of contact with the atmosphere for centuries . Carbon that is buried in sediment can be locked away for millennia or longer . The three "lanes" of the pump Gravitational pump: sinking particles (marine snow). Migrant pump: animals that feed at the surface at night and respire or excrete at depth during the day. Mixing pump: dissolved and suspended organic carbon carried down by seasonal mixing and subduction. Why the twilight zone matters # How efficiently marine snow is consumed between 200 and 1,000 m largely decides how much carbon is sequestered. Small changes in that attenuation shift the ocean’s carbon storage by large amounts. That is why the mesopelagic is a major research focus, and why proposals to fish twilight-zone animals at scale raise concern. The seafloor as a carbon store # Marine sediments, especially muddy coastal shelves and margins, hold enormous stocks of organic carbon. Disturbing them can remineralise that carbon back to CO₂: Bottom trawling: one modelling study estimated that 55–60% of the CO₂ released into seawater by trawling reaches the atmosphere within 7–9 years 3 . The size of these emissions is actively debated (see Bottom trawling ). Deep-sea mining would disturb abyssal sediments, which are carbon-poor but extremely slow to recover. Feedbacks with climate change # Warming and stratification reduce nutrient supply to the surface, which can weaken production in many regions. Acidification affects calcifying plankton, whose mineral shells help ballast sinking particles (see Acidification ). Deoxygenation changes how organic matter is decomposed at depth. Open questions # How large is the migrant pump globally? Estimates vary widely. Is ocean CO₂ uptake weakening as acidification intensifies? A 2025 study suggested it is 2 . t: Life in the Dark: How Deep-Sea Animals Survive
d: The five big survival problems of the deep sea (pressure, darkness, cold, scarce food and finding a mate) and the solutions evolution found for each.
x: The deep sea is Earth’s largest habitat by volume, yet every animal living there faces the same five problems. Looking at the solutions together explains why deep-sea creatures look the way they do. 1. Crushing pressure # Pressure reaches more than 1,000 atmospheres in trenches. Animals cope with piezolytes such as TMAO that stabilise proteins, with flexible membranes rich in unsaturated fats, and by avoiding gas spaces altogether (snailfish have no swim bladder) 1 . See Pressure, light and temperature . 2. Darkness # No sunlight reaches below ~1,000 m. Responses include: Huge or tubular eyes in the twilight zone (barreleye, giant squid with the largest eyes of any animal). Bioluminescence : an estimated majority of mid-water animals make light. They use it for lures, counter-illumination camouflage, signalling and “burglar alarms” (see Bioluminescence ). Black or red colouring , which is invisible in the absence of red light. Some dragonfishes have ultra-black skin absorbing over 99.5% of light. 3. Cold # Below the thermocline the water sits at ~0–4 °C. Metabolism slows, so many species grow slowly, mature late and live long. Orange roughy live over 150 years and Greenland sharks perhaps several centuries. 4. Scarce food # Almost all food sinks from above as marine snow, and only a small fraction reaches the abyss. Strategies: Strategy Example Sit-and-wait ambush with lures Anglerfish, tripod fish Huge mouths and expandable stomachs Gulper eel, viperfish, black swallower Opportunistic scavenging of food falls Giant isopods, hagfish, amphipods Long fasting Giant isopods can survive years without food Chemosynthesis instead of food from above Tubeworms, vent mussels, scaly-foot snail Vertical migration to feed at the surface Lanternfish, krill 5. Finding a mate # In a vast dark ocean with low population densities, encounters are rare. Evolutionary answers include dwarf males that track females by smell (anglerfish, Osedax), hermaphroditism so any encounter can produce offspring (tripod fish), and sperm storage . Gigantism and dwarfism # Some deep-sea groups grow far larger than their shallow relatives ( deep-sea gigantism ): giant isopods, giant amphipods, the colossal squid. Proposed explanations include cold temperatures (larger cell size), higher oxygen solubility in cold water, and efficiency for travelling between scarce food. Others are tiny: meiofauna dominate deep sediments by number. Browse the animals # See the Species Atlas for individual profiles covering feeding, hunting, mating, migration and behaviour. d: Why most deep mid-water animals make their own light, how the chemistry works, and the six main ways they use it.
x: Below 1,000 m, the only light comes from living things. Bioluminescence has evolved independently many dozens of times, so it is a striking example of convergent evolution . The chemistry # Light comes from a reaction between a light-emitting molecule ( luciferin ) and an enzyme ( luciferase ) in the presence of oxygen. The most common marine luciferin, coelenterazine, is shared across many unrelated groups, which may obtain it from their diet. Most deep-sea light is blue-green (~470–490 nm) , the wavelengths that travel furthest in seawater. Animals produce light either themselves or by housing symbiotic luminous bacteria (anglerfish lures, flashlight fish). Six main uses # Functions of bioluminescence Lure prey : anglerfish esca, dragonfish chin barbels. Counter-illumination : belly photophores match downwelling light to erase the animal’s silhouette (lanternfish, hatchetfish, many squid). Defence and startle : sudden flashes, or glowing ink or mucus clouds (vampire squid ejects luminous mucus). “Burglar alarm” : light that attracts a bigger predator to your attacker (Atolla jellyfish, dinoflagellates). Communication and mating : species-specific photophore patterns (lanternfish). Illumination : red-light searchlights in some dragonfishes, invisible to most prey. The burglar-alarm jellyfish that found the giant squid # When attacked, the deep-sea jelly Atolla produces a spinning ring of blue light. In 2012, researchers mimicked this with an LED lure called the “e-jelly”. It helped film the giant squid in its natural habitat for the first time. See Giant squid . At the surface: glowing seas # Coastal “sea sparkle” comes from dinoflagellates that flash when water is disturbed. See Bioluminescent dinoflagellates . Why it matters for science # Luciferases and fluorescent proteins from marine animals, such as green fluorescent protein (GFP) from a jellyfish, became essential tools in biology. The 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded for GFP. Open questions # How many deep-sea species are luminous? Estimates for mid-water animals are high, but seafloor fauna are less studied. How do animals avoid being seen while they glow? Counter-illumination, colour control and ultra-black skin are part of the answer.

d: How fishes conquered the twilight, midnight and hadal zones, from lanternfish swarms to the snailfish depth limit.
x: Fishes live from the surface to about 8,300 m . The deepest is a snailfish filmed at 8,336 m in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench in 2022 1 . Below that, pressure physiology appears to exclude them. By zone # Zone Typical fishes Lifestyle Twilight (200–1,000 m) Lanternfish, hatchetfish, bristlemouths, barreleye Vertical migrators; counter-illumination; large eyes Midnight (1,000–4,000 m) Anglerfish, gulper eels, viperfish, dragonfish Sit-and-wait; lures; huge mouths; weak muscles Abyssal seafloor Grenadiers (rattails), cusk eels, tripod fish Scavenging and hunting near the bottom Hadal (6,000–8,300 m) Snailfishes (Liparidae) Trench specialists; top predators on amphipods Bristlemouths ( Cyclothone ) may be the most numerous vertebrates on Earth, possibly hundreds of trillions, yet few people have heard of them. Deep vs shallow fish # Trait Deep-sea fish Shallow-water fish Metabolism Low High Muscles and skeleton Reduced, watery Strong, dense Colour Black, red or transparent Bright signalling colours Senses Lateral line, smell, large or tubular eyes Colour vision dominant Reproduction Rare encounters: dwarf males, hermaphroditism Spawning aggregations, courtship displays See the repository’s deep vs shallow fish comparative notes figure: The 8,200 m limit # Fishes accumulate TMAO to protect proteins from pressure. Concentrations rise linearly with depth and would make fish tissues hyperosmotic to seawater at around 8,200 m. Observations fit: fish are common to ~7,000–8,000 m and absent below about 8,400 m 1 . See Hadal life . Explore the fishes # Browse profiles in the Species Atlas , including the anglerfish, viperfish, barreleye, tripod fish, coelacanth, orange roughy and Mariana snailfish. t: Hadal Life: Living at the Bottom of the World
d: Trenches deeper than 6,000 m host snailfish, giant amphipods and, as of 2025, flourishing chemosynthetic communities at 9,533 m.
x: The hadal zone , the ocean trenches from 6,000 to ~11,000 m, makes up a tiny fraction of the seafloor but spans almost half the ocean’s depth range. Each trench is an isolated, extreme habitat. Many host endemic species. Key records Deepest fish filmed: a Pseudoliparis snailfish at 8,336 m , Izu-Ogasawara Trench (2022) 1 . Deepest fish caught: P. belyaevi at 8,022 m , Japan Trench 1 . Deepest chemosynthetic animal community: tubeworms and bivalves at 9,533 m , Kuril–Kamchatka Trench ( Nature , 2025) 2 . Deepest plastic bag: 10,898 m , Mariana Trench 3 . Who lives there # Snailfishes : the top fish predators, translucent and scaleless. Amphipods : scavenging crustaceans. Hirondellea gigas in the Challenger Deep can digest wood using enzymes. Giant amphipods ( Alicella gigantea ) reach ~30 cm. Holothurians (sea cucumbers) : often dominate trench floors by biomass. Xenophyophores : giant single-celled organisms. Chemosynthetic communities : siboglinid tubeworms and bivalves fed by methane and sulfide seeping along faults in the bending plate 2 . The 2025 discovery # The crewed submersible Fendouzhe surveyed the Kuril–Kamchatka and western Aleutian trenches in July–August 2024. It found chemosynthesis-based communities over ~2,500 km at 5,800–9,533 m , with high sediment methane likely made by microbes in place 2 . That changes the picture of trench ecosystems from food-starved basins to places that can host methane-powered oases. Full analysis: Peng et al. 2025 . Why trenches funnel food (and pollution) # The V-shape of trenches concentrates organic matter sliding down the slopes, and earthquakes trigger sediment avalanches. That supports surprising biomass, but it also concentrates pollutants . PCBs and microplastics have been found in hadal amphipods. Exploration # Only a handful of crewed dives have reached the deepest points: Trieste (1960), Deepsea Challenger (2012), Limiting Factor (2019 onwards) and Fendouzhe (2020 onwards). See History of exploration . t: Chemosynthetic Ecosystems: Vents, Seeps and Whale Falls
d: Entire food webs powered not by sunlight but by chemical energy, discovered only in 1977 and still yielding new species and depth records.
x: In 1977 the submersible Alvin found dense animal communities around hydrothermal vents on the Galápagos Rift. This was the first evidence of ecosystems that do not depend on sunlight . Microbes there harvest chemical energy ( chemosynthesis ) from compounds like hydrogen sulfide, methane and hydrogen. Three kinds of chemosynthetic habitat # Habitat Energy source Lifespan Iconic fauna Hydrothermal vents Hot fluids rich in H₂S, H₂, metals Years to decades (volcanically reset) Giant tubeworms, Pompeii worms, yeti crabs, scaly-foot snail Cold seeps Methane and sulfide seeping from sediments Centuries to millennia Seep mussels, clams, tubeworms, ice worms on methane hydrate Food falls (whale, wood) Decomposing organic matter producing sulfide Years to decades Osedax bone worms, hagfish, wood-boring bivalves Symbiosis is the key # Most large chemosynthetic animals host bacteria inside their bodies . The giant tubeworm Riftia has no mouth or gut as an adult; a specialised organ holds billions of sulfur-oxidising bacteria fed by a special sulfide-carrying haemoglobin. See Giant tube worm . A whale fall’s life cycle # Mobile scavenger stage (months to years): sharks, hagfish and amphipods strip the flesh. Enrichment-opportunist stage (years): worms and crustaceans colonise the enriched sediment. Osedax bores into the bones. Sulfophilic stage (decades): bacteria decompose bone lipids, producing sulfide that supports chemosynthetic communities. Records and discoveries # Deepest chemosynthetic animal community: 9,533 m (Kuril–Kamchatka Trench, Nature 2025) 1 . See Hadal life . Lost City (Mid-Atlantic Ridge): carbonate chimneys up to 60 m, powered by serpentinisation rather than magma. It is a leading model for the origin of life. Why it matters beyond Earth # Chemosynthesis shows that life can run on rock–water chemistry in total darkness. That is exactly the kind of energy that might exist in the subsurface oceans of Europa and Enceladus . Threats # Seafloor massive sulfide deposits that form at vents are potential mining targets. The vent-endemic scaly-foot snail was listed as Endangered by the IUCN because its few known vent fields lie within exploration licences. See Deep-sea mining . t: Species Discovery: How Many Ocean Species Are Still Unknown?
d: The Ocean Census, eDNA and a new "discovered" status are speeding up the naming of ocean life, but most species remain undescribed.
x: About 240,000 marine species have been formally described. Estimates of the total range far higher, and some studies suggest up to ~90% of ocean species remain undiscovered 5 . New marine species recorded by the Ocean Census 728 Usual yearly rate (approx.) 1,121 Apr 2025–Mar 2026 Source: Nekton / Ocean Census (+54%) The Ocean Census # The Nippon Foundation–Nekton Ocean Census is the largest coordinated effort to speed up marine species discovery. Year 3 (1 Apr 2025 – 31 Mar 2026) 1,121 species new to science recorded, a 54% increase over the usual annual rate 1 . 13 expeditions and 9 species-discovery workshops 2 . About two-thirds (728) came through Species Discovery Awards. Many came from specimens already sitting in museum collections 3 . Highlights included new ghost sharks, a carnivorous Chondrocladia “death-ball” sponge at ~3,600 m, and a polychaete living inside a glass sponge at 791 m. The description bottleneck # Formal scientific description takes an average of ~13.5 years from discovery to publication 4 . To avoid species going extinct before they have a name, the Ocean Census launched NOVA , an open platform where “discovered” is recorded immediately as a formal status. New tools # eDNA: genetic traces in water reveal species without capturing them. 4K and 8K ROV video with AI-assisted annotation (for example MBARI’s archives). Integrative taxonomy: combining genomes, micro-CT scans and morphology. Why it matters # Unnamed species cannot be protected or assessed. New species are being found in areas earmarked for deep-sea mining , where most fauna are undescribed. See Deep-sea mining . d: The deepest places on Earth form where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. Here are their geology, the record holders and why they matter.
x: Ocean trenches are long, narrow depressions where an oceanic plate subducts beneath another plate. They hold all of Earth’s deepest points and most of the hadal zone (>6,000 m). Deepest trenches # Trench Ocean Max depth (approx.) Mariana (Challenger Deep) Pacific ~10,935 m Tonga (Horizon Deep) Pacific ~10,800 m Kuril–Kamchatka Pacific ~9,600 m Philippine (Galathea Depth) Pacific ~10,500 m Kermadec Pacific ~10,000 m Izu-Ogasawara Pacific ~9,800 m Puerto Rico (Milwaukee Deep) Atlantic ~8,400 m South Sandwich (Factorian Deep) Southern ~7,400 m Java (Sunda) Indian ~7,290 m How trenches work # As the down-going plate bends, it cracks into normal faults. These faults channel fluids, and in the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench they feed methane seeps that support chemosynthetic life down to 9,533 m 1 . Subduction also drives the largest earthquakes (megathrust events such as Tōhoku 2011 and Sumatra 2004), tsunamis, and the volcanic arcs of the Pacific Ring of Fire. Trenches as sinks # The trench shape funnels sediment, organic carbon and pollution downslope. Trenches store organic carbon at higher rates than the surrounding abyss, and they accumulate plastics and persistent pollutants. Life # See Hadal life : snailfish, giant amphipods, sea cucumbers, xenophyophores and chemosynthetic oases. t: Hydrothermal Vents and Cold Seeps: The Geology
d: How seawater circulating through hot ocean crust builds black smokers, white smokers and carbonate towers, and how seeps differ.
x: At mid-ocean ridges, back-arc basins and hotspots, seawater seeps into cracks in young crust, is heated by magma to 350–400 °C , picks up metals and sulfide, and gushes back out. Vent types # Type Temperature Look Chemistry Black smoker 350–400 °C Black clouds of metal sulfide particles; tall chimneys Acidic, metal- and sulfide-rich White smoker 100–300 °C Lighter particles (barium, calcium, silicon) Cooler, often at field margins Diffuse flow 5–100 °C Shimmering water from cracks Supports most of the biomass Alkaline/serpentinite (e.g. Lost City) 40–90 °C White carbonate towers up to 60 m Hydrogen- and methane-rich from rock–water reactions Fluids stay liquid at these temperatures because of the immense pressure. Cold seeps # Seeps occur along continental margins and trenches where methane- and sulfide-rich fluids leak slowly from sediments. They are cooler and longer-lived than vents, with features such as methane hydrate mounds , brine pools and authigenic carbonate pavements. Mineral deposits # Vent chimneys build seafloor massive sulfide (SMS) deposits rich in copper, zinc, gold and silver, which is why vents attract mining interest (see Deep-sea mining ). Life # See Chemosynthetic ecosystems .

d: Underwater volcanoes that are biodiversity oases, and the vast flat plains that cover most of the ocean floor.
x: Seamounts # Seamounts are underwater mountains, mostly extinct volcanoes, that rise at least 1,000 m above the seafloor without breaking the surface. Estimates suggest there are tens of thousands of large seamounts, most of them never visited. Why they are oases: seamounts deflect currents, causing local upwelling and trapping plankton. That supports cold-water corals, sponges, and aggregations of fish such as orange roughy , alongside sharks, tuna and seabirds above. Vulnerability: seamount fisheries in the 1980s–90s stripped coral habitats that will take centuries or millennia to regrow. Cobalt-rich crusts on seamount flanks are also potential mining targets. Abyssal plains # At 3,000–6,000 m, abyssal plains are among the flattest surfaces on Earth, built by sediments that blanket the underlying crust. They cover a large fraction of the ocean floor. Food: very little. The fauna depends on marine snow and seasonal pulses of phytodetritus. Fauna: sea cucumbers (sea pigs), brittle stars, xenophyophores, nematodes and polychaete worms. Diversity is surprisingly high but densities are low. Nodule fields: polymetallic nodules cover large parts of some plains, especially the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (see Polymetallic nodules ). Exploration gap: abyssal plains and seamounts are among the least visually explored habitats 1 . Ocean Discovery League / EurekAlert release on Bell et al. 2025 — https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1082535   ↩

d: Three unusual deep habitats: sediment highways cut into continental margins, glacier-carved deep inlets, and lakes at the bottom of the sea.
x: Submarine canyons # Canyons cut into continental shelves and slopes, some rivalling the Grand Canyon. They act as highways carrying sediment, organic matter (and litter) from the coast to the abyss, often via turbidity currents. They are biodiversity hotspots, and some, such as Monterey Canyon , are among the best-studied deep habitats on Earth. Monterey alone accounts for ~48% of all canyon observations, and only 442 of 9,472 known canyons have ever been seen 1 . Fjords # Glaciers carved deep, steep inlets now flooded by the sea. Shallow sills at the mouth trap deep water, which can become low in oxygen. Norwegian fjords host cold-water coral reefs at unusually shallow depths, so deep-sea species can be studied near the surface. Brine pools # Where ancient salt deposits dissolve beneath the seafloor (Gulf of Mexico, Red Sea, Mediterranean), extremely dense brine collects in depressions. These “lakes” have their own shorelines and waves. Salinity can be several times that of seawater, and the brine is often anoxic and methane-rich. Animals that swim in can be killed and pickled. The Gulf of Mexico’s “Jacuzzi of Despair” is ringed by mussels feeding on methane at its edge. Microbes inside are studied as analogues for possible life on Mars and icy moons. Gigazine summary of Bell et al. 2025 (canyon observation statistics) — https://wbgsv0a.gigazine.net/gsc_news/en/20250518-deep-seafloor-study-reveals   ↩

d: Potato-sized mineral lumps that grow a few millimetres per million years, now at the centre of the deep-sea mining fight.
x: Polymetallic (manganese) nodules are concretions of manganese and iron oxides enriched in nickel, copper, cobalt and rare earths. They grow around a nucleus (such as a shark tooth or rock fragment) by a few millimetres per million years , so a nodule can be tens of millions of years old. Where # The richest field is the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ) in the Pacific, an abyssal plain of more than 6 million km² at ~4,000–6,000 m. It is estimated to hold over 21 billion tonnes of nodules 1 . Other fields lie in the Indian Ocean (the Central Indian Ocean Basin, where India holds an ISA exploration contract) and the Peru Basin. Life on nodules # Nodules are hard islands on a soft plain. Many sponges, corals, anemones and xenophyophores only live attached to them. Removing nodules removes that habitat for geological timescales. After 44 years, a 1979 test-mining track still shows these attached animals barely returning 2 . See Jones et al. 2025 . “Dark oxygen” # In 2024, benthic chamber experiments reported oxygen being produced on nodule fields. The authors proposed that nodule surfaces act like batteries, splitting seawater by electrolysis. The claim is contested, and a dedicated follow-up programme (DORI) began in 2026 3 . See Sweetman et al. 2024 . The mining case # Nodules contain battery metals. Proponents argue nodule collection avoids some land-mining impacts. Opponents point to irreversible habitat loss, sediment plumes over wide areas, and unknown ecosystem functions. See Deep-sea mining . Heriot-Watt University, deep-sea mining impacts (CCZ size and nodule tonnage) — https://www.hw.ac.uk/news/2025/deep-sea-mining-for-rare-metals-impacts-marine-life-for-decades-scientists-say   ↩ NHM press release, Jones et al. 2025 Nature — https://nhm.ac.uk/press-office/press-releases/new-study-reveals-long-term-impacts-of-deep-sea-mining-and-first3.html   ↩ SAMS, Dark Oxygen Research Initiative — https://sams.ac.uk/science/projects/dori/   ↩

d: 150 years from a sounding line on HMS Challenger to crewed full-ocean-depth submersibles, told through the milestones that changed what we know.
x: Timeline at a glance 1872–1876 : HMS Challenger expedition sounds the deep with weighted ropes, discovers thousands of new species and records a ~8,000 m depth in the Mariana region. It founds modern oceanography. 1930–1934 : Bathysphere : William Beebe and Otis Barton descend to 923 m off Bermuda and see deep-sea bioluminescence first-hand. 1951 : HMS Challenger II uses echo sounding to locate the deepest point, later named the Challenger Deep . 1960 : Bathyscaphe Trieste (Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh) reaches the bottom of the Challenger Deep. 1964 : DSV Alvin enters service. It goes on to make thousands of dives and is still operating after upgrades. 1977 : Alvin finds hydrothermal vent communities on the Galápagos Rift, the first life powered by chemosynthesis. 1985 : The Titanic wreck is found (3,800 m) with towed camera systems. 2000 : Lost City hydrothermal field is discovered on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. 2012 : James Cameron makes a solo dive to the Challenger Deep in Deepsea Challenger . The giant squid is filmed in its habitat. 2017 : Seabed 2030 launches with only ~6% of the seafloor mapped to modern standards. 2019 : Limiting Factor (Five Deeps Expedition) reaches the deepest point of every ocean and begins repeat full-depth diving. 2020 : China's Fendouzhe reaches the Challenger Deep with a crew of three. 2022 : The deepest fish is filmed (snailfish, 8,336 m). 2024 : Fendouzhe finds chemosynthetic communities to 9,533 m (published 2025). 2026 : Seabed 2030 reaches 28.7% mapped. The Ocean Census reports 1,121 new species in a year. Record crewed dives (metres) 923 Bathysphere 1934 10,916 Trieste 1960 10,908 Deepsea Challenger 2012 10,925 Limiting Factor 2019 10,909 Fendouzhe 2020 Source: Expedition records Four eras # Sounding and dredging (1870s–1920s): ropes, wires and nets. The Challenger expedition dispelled the “azoic hypothesis” that no life exists below ~550 m. Acoustics and bathyscaphes (1920s–1960s): echo sounders revealed the shape of ocean basins, including the mid-ocean ridges that led to plate tectonics. Trieste proved humans could reach the bottom. Submersibles and discovery (1964–2000s): Alvin and its peers found vents, seeps and whale-fall communities. ROVs took over much routine work. Full-depth and data era (2010s–now): repeatable full-ocean-depth crewed dives, autonomous vehicles, telepresence expeditions streamed live, eDNA and AI-assisted video annotation. Lessons # Every era overturned an assumption: that the deep was lifeless, that life needs sunlight, that trenches are barren, that fish can live anywhere. Yet only about 0.001% of the deep seafloor has been seen 1 . See How little we have seen . Bell et al. 2025, Science Advances — https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adp8602   ↩

d: HOVs, ROVs, AUVs, landers and floats compared, with what each is best at and the engineering behind surviving 1,000+ atmospheres.
x: Platform What it is Strengths Limits Examples HOV (human-occupied vehicle) Crewed submersible with a pressure sphere Human observation, dexterous sampling, public impact Expensive, short bottom times, risk Alvin (to 6,500 m), Fendouzhe and Limiting Factor (full depth), Shinkai 6500, Matsya 6000 (India, in development) ROV (remotely operated vehicle) Tethered robot piloted from a ship Long dives, high-power tools, live HD video, telepresence Needs a large ship and tether SuBastian, Isis, Okeanos Explorer’s Deep Discoverer, MBARI’s Doc Ricketts AUV (autonomous underwater vehicle) Untethered pre-programmed robot High-resolution mapping close to the seafloor; wide coverage Limited real-time control Sentry, Autosub, Orpheus Lander Instrument frame dropped to the seafloor Long-duration measurements, baited cameras, chemistry chambers Fixed position Hadal landers (deepest fish records), dark-oxygen chambers Floats and gliders Profiling floats and buoyancy-driven gliders Global ocean monitoring for years Mostly upper 2,000 m (Deep Argo to 6,000 m) Argo network (~4,000 floats) Engineering for pressure # Pressure hulls: titanium spheres, often 7–9 cm thick for full ocean depth. Composite hulls have failed catastrophically (the Titan implosion in 2023). Buoyancy: syntactic foam made of glass microballoons in epoxy. Oil-compensated systems let motors and electronics sit in oil at ambient pressure instead of in heavy housings. Communication: acoustic modems underwater (low bandwidth), and fibre-optic tethers for ROVs. India’s deep-ocean programme # India’s Deep Ocean Mission includes Samudrayaan , which plans to carry three people to 6,000 m in the Matsya 6000 submersible being developed by the National Institute of Ocean Technology. India also holds an ISA nodule exploration contract in the Central Indian Ocean Basin. Trends # Telepresence: expeditions streamed live with remote scientists ashore. Low-cost cameras and landers to widen who explores. AI for automated species detection in video.

d: Why we have better maps of Mars than of our own seafloor, how multibeam sonar works, and whether Seabed 2030 can finish the job.
x: Seafloor mapped to modern resolution (Seabed 2030) (%) 0 5 10 15 20 25 30 2017 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 Jun 2025 Apr 2026 2017: 6% 2019: 15% 2020: 19% 2021: 20.6% 2022: 23.4% 2023: 24.9% 2024: 26.1% Jun 2025: 27.3% Apr 2026: 28.7% Source: Nippon Foundation–GEBCO Seabed 2030; IHO Methods # Satellite altimetry: sea-surface height bulges over seamounts and dips over trenches. This gives a global map, but only at ~kilometre resolution. Multibeam echo sounding: ships emit a fan of sound beams and time the echoes, mapping a swath several times the water depth wide at ~100 m resolution or better in the deep sea. AUV mapping: flying close to the seabed for metre-scale resolution. Crowd-sourced bathymetry: fishing boats, yachts and commercial ships contribute depth data. Seabed 2030 progress # Numbers 6% mapped to modern standards at launch in 2017 1 . 27.3% by June 2025 1 . 28.7% by April 2026, with almost five million km² added in a year, about 104 million km² in total 2 . Will it finish by 2030? # At ~1.5 percentage points per year, no. Reaching 100% would need roughly an order-of-magnitude acceleration. Uncrewed surface vessels, data-sharing from industry and militaries, and crowd-sourcing are the main levers. Even complete mapping at ~100 m resolution would not show what lives there; imaging coverage is far smaller (see How little we have seen ). Why maps matter # Tsunami modelling, cable routing, navigation, fisheries habitat models, climate models (bottom topography steers currents) and deciding where to protect. d: Only about 0.001% of the deep seafloor has ever been imaged, and almost all of it near three countries. Here is what that bias means.
x: The numbers (Bell et al. 2025, Science Advances) Total deep seafloor ever imaged: about 2,130–3,823 km² , which is ≤0.001% of ~336 million km² 1 . Built from ~ 44,000 dives since 1958 2 . 65% of observations lie within 200 nautical miles of the USA, Japan and New Zealand . 97% of dives come from five countries 3 . Even if the estimate is off by 10×, less than 0.01% would have any visual record 4 . How much of the deep seafloor we know Mapped (any resolution, satellite) Mapped (any resolution, satellite) 100% Mapped at modern resolution (2026) Mapped at modern resolution (2026) 28.7% Ever seen by a camera Ever seen by a camera 0.001% Source: Bell et al. 2025; Seabed 2030 Biases # Geographic: waters off a handful of wealthy nations dominate. Habitat: canyons and ridges are over-sampled. Abyssal plains and seamounts are under-sampled. Monterey Canyon alone accounts for ~48% of canyon observations 5 . Depth: most of the ocean lies at 2,000–6,000 m, but dives cluster shallower. What it means # “Typical deep-sea fauna” is generalised from a sample the size of a small city. Mining impact assessments rest on thin baselines. Low-cost exploration tools and partnerships with under-represented nations are essential. Read the full paper analysis: Bell et al. 2025 . d: The ocean absorbs over 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases. 2025 set a ninth straight record, with about 23 ZJ added in one year.
x: The ocean is where global warming really accumulates. Over 90% of the excess energy trapped by greenhouse gases ends up in seawater. That makes ocean heat content (OHC) one of the most reliable indicators of climate change, because it is far less noisy than air temperature 1 . 2025 in numbers (Pan, Cheng et al. 2026, Adv. Atmos. Sci.) Upper 2,000 m OHC rose by ~23 ± 8 zettajoules relative to 2024 2 . That made 2025 the ninth consecutive record year , the longest streak on record 3 . The 2024 gain was about 16 ZJ (other estimates put it near 13 ZJ), so 2025 was markedly larger 3 4 . 23 ZJ is roughly 200 times humanity’s annual electricity consumption 1 . Regions at record heat included the tropical and South Atlantic, Mediterranean, North Indian Ocean and Southern Ocean 3 . This happened despite developing La Niña conditions, which usually cool the surface 2 . Heat added to the upper 2,000 m of the ocean in one year 16 ZJ 2024 23 ZJ 2025 1 ZJ = 10²¹ joules. 23 ZJ ≈ 200× humanity's annual electricity use. Source: Pan, Cheng et al. 2026 via Eos Why heat goes deep # Argo floats measure the upper 2,000 m, and most added heat sits there. But heat is now detected in the abyss too, carried down where deep water forms near Antarctica and in the North Atlantic. Deep Argo floats (to 6,000 m) are extending the record. Consequences # Sea-level rise: warm water expands. Thermal expansion is a major share of sea-level rise. Marine heatwaves: more frequent, longer and deeper, driving coral bleaching and mass die-offs. Stronger storms: warmer surface water fuels tropical cyclones. Less oxygen: warmer water holds less gas and stratifies more (see Deoxygenation ). Habitat shifts: species move poleward and deeper. Open question # How quickly do surface heatwaves propagate into the twilight zone (200–1,000 m), where most fish biomass lives? Recent compound-change analyses show deep-reaching changes over 60 years, but direct observation remains sparse 4 . d: The ocean has absorbed about a quarter of human CO₂ emissions, and in 2025 scientists concluded the acidification planetary boundary was crossed around 2020.
x: When CO₂ dissolves in seawater it forms carbonic acid. This lowers pH and, critically, reduces the carbonate ions that corals, shellfish, pteropods and many plankton need to build shells and skeletons. The usual measure is aragonite saturation state (Ω arag ) . Planetary boundary crossed Findlay et al. (2025, Global Change Biology ) reassessed the ocean acidification boundary, defined as a 20% drop in Ω arag from pre-industrial levels. They found the global ocean entered the boundary’s uncertainty range by 2020 1 . Over 40% of the surface ocean and up to 60% of the upper 200 m had crossed it 1 . Suitable habitat has fallen by 43% for tropical and subtropical coral reefs, up to 61% for polar pteropods and 13% for coastal bivalves 1 . The authors propose a safer 10% boundary, which the entire surface ocean passed around 2000 1 . The 2025 Planetary Health Check also counted ocean acidification as crossed, bringing the total to seven of nine boundaries 2 . Why the deep is exposed # Subsurface waters are changing faster than expected , so impacts may be worse than surface data suggest. The aragonite saturation horizon , below which shells dissolve, is getting shallower. That squeezes the habitat of cold-water corals such as Desmophyllum pertusum , many of which already live close to this horizon. Polar waters are most affected because cold water dissolves more CO₂. Who is affected # Organism Effect Pteropods (sea butterflies) Shell dissolution; key food for salmon and whales Corals (shallow and deep) Slower calcification; weaker reef frameworks Oysters, mussels, scallops Larval failure; documented hatchery losses Coccolithophores, foraminifera Thinner plates; changes to the carbon pump Fish Altered senses and behaviour in some experiments (debated) Outlook # Without rapid emission cuts, nearly all of the surface ocean is projected to exceed safe acidity levels by 2100 under mid- to high-emission scenarios 3 . Unlike warming, acidification cannot be offset by reflecting sunlight. Only cutting CO₂ fixes it. Findlay, Feely, Jiang, Pelletier & Bednaršek 2025, Global Change Biology 31(6): e70238, doi:10.1111/gcb.70238 (OA-ICC summary) — https://news-oceanacidification-icc.org/2025/06/20/ocean-acidification-another-planetary-boundary-crossed/   ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩ Dialogue Earth, “Ocean acidification boundary crossed” — https://dialogue.earth/en/digest/ocean-acidification-boundary-crossed/   ↩ To Vima, coverage of the study’s projections — https://www.tovima.com/climate/ocean-acidification-crossed-a-critical-threshold-scientists-warn/amp/   ↩

d: The ocean has lost more than 2% of its oxygen since 1960, the volume of anoxic water has quadrupled, and oxygen minimum zones are growing.
x: Oxygen loss is the least-known of the ocean’s three climate stressors (with warming and acidification), but it may be just as dangerous. Key measurements Global ocean oxygen fell by more than 2% (4.8 ± 2.1 petamoles) between 1960 and 2010, from a total of ~227 petamoles (Schmidtko et al. 2017, Nature ) 1 . The volume of oxygen-free water in the open ocean has quadrupled 2 . Oxygen minimum zones at 200 m expanded by ~4.5 million km² , roughly 60% of Australia’s area 3 . Coastal areas at risk of dead zones have grown more than tenfold since 1950 2 . Losses could reach up to 7% by 2100 4 . Ocean oxygen loss Global ocean O₂ lost since 1960 Global ocean O₂ lost since 1960 2% Projected loss by 2100 (high emissions) Projected loss by 2100 (high emiss… 7% About 15% of the observed loss is because warmer water holds less gas; the rest comes from weaker mixing. Source: Schmidtko et al. 2017; projections Why oxygen is falling # Solubility: warm water holds less gas. This explains about 15% of the loss 1 . Stratification: a warmer surface layer mixes less with deeper water, so less oxygen is carried down. Weaker overturning (see AMOC weakening ) adds to this. Nutrient pollution (coastal): fertiliser and sewage fuel algal blooms whose decay consumes oxygen. Oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) # OMZs are natural mid-water layers (roughly 100–1,000 m) beneath productive surface waters, especially in the eastern tropical Pacific, Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. As they expand: Tuna, billfish and sharks are squeezed into shallower water, where they are easier to catch. Microbes in OMZs produce nitrous oxide , a potent greenhouse gas, and remove fixed nitrogen. Specialists such as the vampire squid thrive in low oxygen, but most animals cannot. The deep connection # Deep water gets oxygen only where it sinks from the surface at high latitudes. Slower overturning means deep habitats such as cold-water coral reefs could lose oxygen, though the size of that effect this century is still debated. Can it reverse? # Some models suggest OMZs may start shrinking from 2150–2300, but only after centuries 5 . Reducing nutrient runoff can shrink coastal dead zones quickly. Open-ocean deoxygenation needs emission cuts. t: Coral Bleaching and the Fourth Global Event
d: Heat stress reached 84.4% of the world's reefs in 2023–2025, the largest bleaching event ever recorded, and the world may now be in an era of near-annual bleaching.
x: Corals live in partnership with symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) that supply most of their food and colour. When water is too warm for too long, corals expel the algae and turn white. If the heat lasts, they starve and die. Global coral bleaching events: reef area under bleaching-level heat stress 21% 1998 37% 2010 68.2% 2014–17 84.4% 2023–25 Source: NOAA Coral Reef Watch Global bleaching events # Event Years Reef area at bleaching-level heat stress 1st 1998 21% 2nd 2010 37% 3rd 2014–2017 68.2% 4th 2023–2025 84.4% , with mass bleaching in ≥83 countries and territories NOAA confirmed the fourth event on 15 April 2024. It likely ended after severe bleaching in Western Australia in early 2025. NOAA confirmed the end only after no widespread bleaching occurred in the Dec 2025–Feb 2026 austral summer (update of 2 June 2026) 1 2 . An era of near-annual bleaching # Every strong El Niño since 1998 has coincided with a global event, and reefs now get too little time to recover between heatwaves. A building El Niño raised concern again in mid-2026. Are deep reefs a refuge? # Mesophotic reefs (30–150 m) were once hoped to be refuges. They help in some places, but heat can reach them through mixing and internal waves. Cold-water corals in the deep sea face a different combination: acidification, deoxygenation and trawling (see Acidification ). What helps # Rapid emission cuts. This is the only long-term fix. Reducing local stressors: pollution, overfishing and sedimentation. Assisted evolution, heat-tolerant coral breeding and restoration. These are promising but small-scale. d: The Atlantic overturning that ventilates the deep North Atlantic is weakening, with new projections of 43–59% decline by 2100 and a live debate about committed collapse.
x: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) carries warm surface water north. There it cools, sinks and flows back south at depth, delivering oxygen and carbon to the deep Atlantic (see Deep circulation ). AMOC strength projections to 2100 (relative to today) (%) 0 20 40 60 80 100 2025 2050 2075 2100 2025: 100% 2050: 82% 2075: 65% 2100: 49% 2025: 100% 2050: 90% 2075: 84% 2100: 80% Observation-constrained (central) Strong emission cuts Source: Portmann et al. 2026 (central ~51% weakening; ~20% with strong cuts); intermediate points interpolated What the 2026 evidence says # Observed: weakening at four latitudes over two decades (University of Miami study, April 2026). Projected (Portmann et al. 2026, Science Advances ): combining models with temperature and salinity observations gives 43–59% weakening by 2100 (central ≈51%). That is about 60% stronger than the multi-model average. Aggressive emission cuts reduce it to about 20%. Greenland meltwater is not included, so this may be an underestimate 1 2 . Committed collapse? A July 2026 ensemble study argues there is a significant probability that collapse is already locked in 3 . Where scientists disagree The IPCC AR6 assessed collapse before 2100 as “very unlikely” (medium confidence). Newer observation-constrained studies argue the risk is higher. Disagreements centre on model biases in salinity, how to read short observational records, and early-warning statistics from proxy data. Consequences of a major slowdown # Colder winters in northwest Europe, despite global warming. Faster sea-level rise along the US East Coast. Shifted tropical rain belts, affecting monsoons in West Africa and South Asia. Less oxygen and carbon reaching the deep North Atlantic , affecting cold-water coral reefs and deep fauna. Reduced ocean uptake of CO₂. Full analysis of the paper: Portmann et al. 2026 . t: Deep-Sea Mining: Science, Law and the 2026 State of Play
d: Nodules, crusts and vent sulfides; the ISA Mining Code that still is not finished; the US permit route; and the evidence each side cites.
x: Three kinds of deep-sea mineral deposit Polymetallic nodules on abyssal plains (nickel, cobalt, copper, manganese): see Polymetallic nodules . Cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts on seamount flanks: see Seamounts . Seafloor massive sulfides at vents (copper, zinc, gold, silver): see Hydrothermal vents . How nodule collection would work # A tracked collector vehicle crawls the seafloor, sucking up the top layer of sediment and nodules. A riser pipe lifts the slurry to a ship, and the sediment-laden water is discharged back into the ocean. The main impacts are habitat removal (nodules and the animals attached to them), sediment plumes near the bottom and at the discharge depth, noise and light , and compaction of the seabed. The policy detail below is kept current in the hub’s governance notes. Status date: November 15, 2026. This is policy context for the science, not a position for or against mining. Arguments on both sides are summarised as their proponents make them. 1. International Seabed Authority (ISA) # Under UNCLOS, the ISA regulates mineral activity in “the Area” (seabed beyond national jurisdiction). Its Mining Code (exploitation regulations) is still unfinished. 31st session: Part I Council: 9–19 March 2026. Part II Council: 13–24 July 2026. More than 200 delegates attended, from 33 of the 36 Council members. Assembly: 27–31 July 2026. Outcome: on 24 July the Council agreed a roadmap of remaining work but did not adopt the Mining Code. No exploitation was approved. Next: 32nd session in 2027. 2. United States route (NOAA / DSHMRA) # NOAA’s final rule creating a consolidated exploration-licence + commercial-recovery-permit process took effect on 21 Jan 2026 . This followed the April 2025 executive order on offshore minerals. TMC announced its consolidated filing on 22 Jan 2026 (NOAA records the application as submitted on 6 Feb 2026). It covers ~65,000 km² of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (up from ~25,000 km² in its April 2025 application). NOAA found the application in substantial compliance (Mar 2026), then full compliance (reported May 2026). It opened public comment and held a virtual hearing on 13 Oct 2026 . Next: if NOAA certifies the application, an Environmental Impact Statement follows, with more public comment. TMC says it expects a permit before the end of Q1 2027. Why it matters: this is a national route that runs parallel to the ISA. Many states argue it conflicts with UNCLOS; the US is not a party to UNCLOS. 3. High Seas Treaty (BBNJ Agreement) # Adopted 19 June 2023. The 60th ratification came on 19 Sep 2025 (Morocco), and it entered into force 17 Jan 2026 . There were 86 parties by mid-March 2026. Tools: high-seas marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, benefit-sharing from marine genetic resources, and capacity building. COP1 must meet within a year of entry into force (expected ~January 2027). Belgium, Chile and China are bidding to host the secretariat. How it interacts with the ISA on seabed mining is still being worked out. The ISA Council deferred a formal BBNJ-cooperation decision. 4. The evidence base both sides cite # Evidence What it found Cited by Jones et al. 2025, Nature (1979 test track, revisited 2023) Tracks and an 8 m cleared strip still sharp after 44 years. Many animals still reduced; some small mobile fauna and xenophyophores returning; large attached fauna (sponges, corals) still rare. Food patchier in tracks. Moratorium advocates (slow recovery) and industry (some recolonisation) Sweetman et al. 2024, Nature Geoscience (“dark oxygen”) Benthic chambers saw O₂ rising over ~2 days on nodule fields. Nodule surfaces showed up to 0.95 V, and the authors propose seawater electrolysis. Moratorium advocates (unknown ecosystem function). TMC disputes the methods, e.g. trapped bubbles. Bell et al. 2025, Sci. Adv. ≤0.001% of the deep seafloor ever imaged Precautionary arguments: baseline knowledge is thin Ocean Census 2026 1,121 new species in one year, many deep Biodiversity is largely undescribed TMC baseline + pilot collection test Industry environmental baseline and the first integrated pilot test since the 1970s Industry: data is sufficient to start and scale responsibly 5. Arguments as their proponents make them # For proceeding (industry, some governments): nodules hold large amounts of nickel, cobalt, manganese and copper for batteries and defence. Supporters argue the land-mining footprint (deforestation, tailings) is worse. They also cite supply security, and a US regulatory track that dates back to 1980–1989 rules. For a moratorium or precautionary pause (dozens of states, many scientists, NGOs): recovery takes decades or more. Most species are undescribed. Sediment plumes and noise would affect wide areas. Ecosystem functions such as possible O₂ production are unknown. Unilateral permits could undermine UNCLOS. Open empirical gaps: plume spread at commercial scale, recovery beyond 44 years, whether dark oxygen exists and matters, and regional biodiversity baselines. d: Dragging weighted nets across the seabed is the most widespread physical disturbance of the deep, with large costs for habitats and possibly the climate.
x: Bottom trawls and dredges are heavy nets and frames dragged across the seafloor to catch fish and shellfish that live on or near the bottom. In terms of area, bottom trawling is the largest human physical disturbance of the seabed . Impacts on habitats # Habitat destruction: cold-water corals, sponge grounds and seamount communities can be flattened in a single pass. Recovery takes decades to millennia. Bycatch: large amounts of non-target animals are caught and discarded. Sediment resuspension: plumes smother filter feeders and change seabed chemistry. Carbon # The trawling carbon question Sala et al. (2021, Nature ) estimated that trawling disturbs sediment carbon equivalent to about 1 Gt of CO₂ per year , comparable to global aviation 1 . They also found that protecting about 4% of the ocean , mostly within national waters, would remove 90% of that risk 2 . Critics argue that much of the remineralised carbon stays in the water rather than reaching the atmosphere. Follow-up work (Atwood et al. 2024) estimated that a large share does reach the atmosphere within about a decade. The magnitude is still debated. A 2026 European study ( Ocean & Coastal Management ) estimated that trawling in EU, UK, Norwegian and Icelandic waters emits ~112 Mt CO₂ per year and costs society up to €16 billion annually , about 90 times the fleet’s profits 3 . About 23% of trawling effort takes place inside European MPAs 4 . Recovery when trawling stops # After a trawling ban in the UK’s Lyme Bay , reef species increased by 95% and juvenile lobsters by 400% 3 . The European Commission aims to phase out bottom-contact fishing in protected areas by 2030 4 . Deep-sea specifics # Deep-sea fish such as orange roughy and roundnose grenadier grow slowly and mature late, so stocks collapse quickly. The UN General Assembly (resolutions from 2006 onwards) calls for protecting vulnerable marine ecosystems (VMEs) . The EU banned bottom trawling below 800 m in its waters in 2016. t: Plastics and Pollution in the Deep
d: From a plastic bag at 10,898 m to microplastics inside vent snails, the deep sea is the final sink for much of the pollution we create.
x: The deep is a plastic sink # Floating plastic accounts for only a small fraction of what enters the ocean. Much of the “missing” plastic ends up on the seafloor 1 . Key findings A plastic bag was found at 10,898 m in the Mariana Trench, the deepest recorded debris 2 . CSIRO estimated about 14 million tonnes of microplastics on the seafloor globally 3 . In 2025, turbidity currents were directly observed carrying microplastics from continental shelves down submarine canyons to the deep sea 4 . Microplastics were found in almost all sampled vent mussels and snails at ~2,000 m in the Indian and southwest Pacific oceans (2026) 5 . A 2025 Nature synthesis mapped microplastics through the whole water column, a “smog” from the surface to the seabed 6 . How plastic gets down # Biofouling: microbes and algae colonise particles, which then sink. Marine snow and faecal pellets package microplastics and carry them down quickly. Turbidity currents and canyons funnel debris downslope. Canyon biodiversity hotspots are now also microplastic hotspots 4 . Bottom currents sort and concentrate fibres in sediment drifts. Other pollutants # PCBs and PBDEs: found in hadal amphipods at concentrations comparable to some polluted coasts. Mercury: reaches deep food webs via sinking particles. “Forever chemicals” (PFAS): carried on microplastic surfaces 4 . Munitions and chemical weapons dumped after the World Wars in the Baltic and elsewhere. Noise: shipping, seismic surveys and (potentially) mining. Why it matters # Deep-sea animals live long and grow slowly, so pollutants accumulate. Deep plastics are effectively impossible to retrieve, which makes prevention at source the only real solution. t: Who Governs the Deep? UNCLOS, the ISA and the High Seas Treaty
d: The legal map of the ocean, covering territorial seas, EEZs, the high seas and "the Area", and the two bodies that now share responsibility for international waters.
x: The legal zones (UNCLOS, 1982) # Zone Distance from coast Who controls what Territorial sea 0–12 nm Full coastal-state sovereignty (with innocent passage for ships) Contiguous zone 12–24 nm Customs, immigration and pollution enforcement Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) Up to 200 nm Coastal state controls fishing, oil, gas and minerals Continental shelf Can extend beyond 200 nm Seabed resources belong to the coastal state High seas Beyond EEZs Water column open to all; covers over 60% of the ocean surface “The Area” Seabed beyond national jurisdiction Minerals are the “common heritage of mankind”, managed by the ISA The International Seabed Authority (ISA) # The ISA is based in Kingston, Jamaica, with 169 members plus the EU. It has issued about 30 exploration contracts for nodules, crusts and sulfides, including India’s contracts in the Central Indian Ocean Basin and the Indian Ocean ridge. It has never approved commercial exploitation. Its Mining Code was still not adopted after the 31st session ended in July 2026. See Deep-sea mining . The High Seas Treaty (BBNJ Agreement) # Status (November 2026) Adopted 19 June 2023. Reached its 60th ratification on 19 September 2025. Entered into force on 17 January 2026 , with 86 parties by March 2026 1 2 . The first Conference of the Parties ( COP1 ) is due by about January 2027. It has four pillars: Area-based management tools , including high-seas marine protected areas . Until now there was no general mechanism to create them. Environmental impact assessments for activities in international waters. Marine genetic resources: sharing benefits from commercial uses of high-seas organisms (for example in drugs and enzymes). Capacity building and technology transfer for developing countries. Open questions # How BBNJ protected areas will interact with the ISA, fisheries bodies and the IMO, each of which keeps its own mandate. Whether the US national mining route undermines UNCLOS (the US is not a party). Whether 30×30 can be reached on the high seas, where only about 1–2% is currently protected (see Marine protected areas ). d: 10% of the ocean is now officially protected, but only about 3% is fully or highly protected, and the high seas lag far behind.
x: The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) set Target 3 : conserve at least 30% of land and sea by 2030 (“30×30”). Where we stand (2026) 10.01% of the ocean is officially designated as protected or conserved. That threshold was first passed in April 2026, up from 8.6% in 2024 1 . About 5 million km² was added in two years, an area larger than the EU 1 . Only about 3.3% is fully or highly protected , with extraction prohibited (MPAtlas, March 2026) 2 . National waters are 23.2% covered, but only 1.7% of areas beyond national jurisdiction are 3 . Only 1.3% of the ocean has protected areas whose management effectiveness has been assessed 1 . How much of the ocean is protected (2026) Target by 2030 (30×30) Target by 2030 (30×30) 30% Designated protected or conserved Designated protected or conserved 10.01% National waters covered National waters covered 23.2% Fully or highly protected Fully or highly protected 3.3% High seas covered High seas covered 1.7% Effectiveness assessed Effectiveness assessed 1.3% Source: IUCN/UNEP-WCMC; MPAtlas; Mongabay Paper parks # Many MPAs allow fishing, including bottom trawling. In the EU, a large share of MPAs are commercially trawled. Strongly protected reserves, by contrast, hold on average several times more fish biomass than fished areas nearby, and “spillover” can benefit neighbouring fisheries. What makes MPAs work # Protection level: fully or highly protected areas deliver most of the benefits. Size and age: large, old, well-enforced reserves perform best. Enforcement: satellite vessel tracking (such as Global Fishing Watch) helps. Connectivity: networks matter because larvae and migrants cross boundaries. Climate-smart design: protecting refuges and corridors as species shift. Deep-sea MPAs # Large remote reserves such as Papahānaumokuākea (USA), the Ross Sea MPA (Antarctica) and the Pitcairn Islands protect huge areas of deep habitat. The High Seas Treaty finally offers a route to protect the open ocean and international seabed (see Who governs the deep? ).
