t: Peng, Du et al. 2025 (Nature): Chemosynthetic Life at 9,533 m
d: Structured analysis of the paper that pushed the known depth of chemosynthetic animal communities to 9,533 m in the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench.
x: How to read this analysis Every analysis follows the same template: citation, access, research question, method, key results, strengths, limitations and critiques, links to the rest of the encyclopedia, an assessment, and follow-ups. Use Open PDF to read a printable copy in a new tab, or Download PDF to save it. Citation: Peng X., Du M., Gebruk A., Mordukhovich V., et al. Nature (published 30 July 2025). doi:10.1038/s41586-025-09317-z Access: 🔓 Open access Analysis basis: abstract, Nature press highlight, IDSSE/CAS release and independent coverage. Full text not read here. Question # Do hadal trenches (6,000–11,000 m) support chemosynthesis-based animal communities, and how deep and widespread are they? Method # Crewed full-ocean-depth submersible Fendouzhe (IDSSE, CAS). Expedition 8 July – 17 August 2024 along the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench, the Kamchatka–Aleutian transition and the western Aleutian Trench. Visual surveys, sampling, and isotopic and geochemical analysis of seep fluids and sediments. Key Results # Dense communities dominated by siboglinid tubeworms and bivalves , fed by hydrogen sulfide and methane seeping from faults where the Pacific Plate bends into the trench. Found over a ~2,500 km region at 5,800–9,533 m . The deepest site (“The Deepest”) is in the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench, at ~98 MPa. Up to ~5,800 tubeworms per m² reported at some sites. Sediment methane was unusually high, consistent with microbes producing methane in place from buried organic carbon. That points to a deep, local carbon recycling loop. The authors suggest similar communities may exist in other trenches with similar geology. Strengths # Direct, crewed observation at record depth, rather than inference from trawls. Large spatial extent (thousands of km) rather than a single spot. Combines biology with fluid geochemistry, which explains why life is there. Limitations and Critiques # It describes one northwest Pacific region. As one independent commentary stressed, it is a regional description, not a global inventory, and it does not quantify the global carbon-cycle role. “Up to 5,800 per m²” is a local peak, not a trench-wide average. Species-level taxonomy of many specimens is likely still in progress. Links to This Hub # Biology: chemosynthesis section in ../biology/deep-sea-animal-biology.md Structure: trenches, in ../structure/natural-structures.md Exploration: depth records table in ../exploration/exploration-methods-and-records.md My Take # This moves hadal chemosynthesis from “a few clam patches” to “possibly a trench-scale ecosystem type”. The most important new idea is the in-situ microbial methane supply. If confirmed elsewhere, trenches are not only sinks for carbon but active bioreactors, and that matters for both carbon budgets and astrobiology analogues. Follow-ups # Repeat surveys in other subduction trenches (Japan, Kermadec, Atacama). Quantify methane flux and the fraction derived from microbes. Compare tubeworm symbiont genomes to vent and seep relatives for pressure adaptation (link to the mutation/ track).

t: Jones et al. 2025 (Nature): 44 Years After a Mining Test
d: What a 1979 nodule-collection track looks like after 44 years, and what it means for mining regulation.
x: How to read this analysis Every analysis follows the same template: citation, access, research question, method, key results, strengths, limitations and critiques, links to the rest of the encyclopedia, an assessment, and follow-ups. Use Open PDF to read a printable copy in a new tab, or Download PDF to save it. Citation: Jones D.O.B., Arias M.B., et al. Nature (published 26 March 2025). doi:10.1038/s41586-025-08921-3 Access: subscription (see the reading list for a full-text route) Analysis basis: press releases from NOC, NHM, Heriot-Watt, Liverpool and SAMS, plus coverage. Full text not read here. Question # What does a deep-sea nodule-mining disturbance look like after four decades, and which parts of the ecosystem recover? Method # The SMARTEX project (NERC-funded) revisited a 1979 industrial test-mining track in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (~5,000 m) in 2023 with RRS James Cook and the ROV Isis . Compared fauna, sediments and food (organic matter) inside the tracks with adjacent unmined seafloor and with nearby plume-affected areas. Key Results # Physical: the tracks look much as they did when made. There is an ~8 m-wide strip cleared of nodules with two furrows from the collector. Biological: abundance and diversity are still substantially lower inside the tracks. Some small, mobile animals on the sediment surface show the first signs of recovery. Xenophyophores (giant single-celled organisms) have recolonised. Large attached fauna such as sponges and corals, many of which need nodules to settle on, remain rare. Food: total food availability is similar, but patchier inside the tracks , which indicates disrupted food resources. Areas affected only by plumes showed more variable, often smaller effects. Strengths # One of the longest real-world time series for a deep-sea mining impact. Multi-indicator: sediments, food webs and several faunal size classes. Limitations and Critiques # A single small test track is far smaller than the hundreds of km² a commercial operation would disturb each year. Recovery from small-scale damage is likely faster than recovery at scale, because colonists can arrive from nearby. The authors note the results don’t decide whether mining is acceptable; they inform protected-area design and monitoring. Nodules take millions of years to form, so nodule-dependent fauna cannot recover on human timescales whatever the sediment does. Links to This Hub # ../governance-and-mining/seabed-governance-2026.md : evidence table Figure: ../governance-and-mining/png/mining_track_recovery_generated.png (qualitative) My Take # Both sides can quote this paper, and both readings are partly right. The clear result is that the habitat-forming layer (nodules plus the attached fauna on them) does not recover on decadal timescales. Any regulation that treats “recolonisation by mobile fauna” as recovery would be misreading it. Follow-ups # Re-survey at 50+ years. Compare with the 2021–22 industry pilot-collector test sites for a modern-equipment baseline. Scale-dependence experiments: does recovery slow with disturbance width?

d: The contested claim that polymetallic nodules produce oxygen in darkness, with the critiques and the DORI follow-up.
x: How to read this analysis Every analysis follows the same template: citation, access, research question, method, key results, strengths, limitations and critiques, links to the rest of the encyclopedia, an assessment, and follow-ups. Use Open PDF to read a printable copy in a new tab, or Download PDF to save it. Citation: Sweetman A.K., et al. (incl. F. Geiger, J.J. Marlow). Nature Geoscience (published 22 July 2024). doi:10.1038/s41561-024-01480-8 Access: 🔓 Open access Analysis basis: abstract, Springer Nature/SAMS releases, coverage of both critiques and responses. Full text not read here. Question # Why did benthic chambers on nodule fields repeatedly record oxygen increasing when deep-sea sediments normally only consume O₂? Method # Benthic lander chamber incubations at ~4,000 m in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone. The chambers enclose seafloor and seawater and log O₂ for up to several days. Cross-checked with a second O₂ measurement method, ex-situ incubations of nodules, and voltage measurements on nodule surfaces. The research was partly funded by mining companies, including TMC. Key Results # In nearly all nodule-field incubations, O₂ rose steadily over ~2 days. Regions without nodules did not show this. Up to 0.95 V was measured on single nodule surfaces. Clustered nodules could plausibly sum higher, past the ~1.23–1.5 V needed to split seawater. Hypothesis: a “geobattery”. Electrochemical seawater splitting on metal-rich nodules releases O₂ (and H₂). Strengths # The anomaly persisted across years and recalibrations, and appeared with two measurement methods. It gives a testable mechanism with clear predictions (H₂ co-production, voltage dependence). Limitations and Critiques # Methodological challenge (TMC and others): possible artefacts such as trapped air bubbles or sensor/chamber effects. Energetics: how could nodules millions of years old sustain enough current? “Batteries run out.” Scale is unknown. The authors themselves say the regional significance can’t be judged from this study. Response: the Dark Oxygen Research Initiative (DORI) , launched Jan 2026 with US$5.2M from the Nippon Foundation, will deploy new landers in another Pacific area. They will measure O₂ and H₂ production, conductivity, turbidity and seafloor respiration, and test microbial versus electrochemical drivers. Links to This Hub # ../governance-and-mining/seabed-governance-2026.md : evidence table ../physics/deep-ocean-physics-chemistry.md : oxygen chemistry My Take # Treat this as a strong anomaly with an unproven mechanism . The key discriminator is hydrogen. Electrolysis must make H₂ alongside O₂ in roughly a 2:1 ratio, while a sensor artefact would not. DORI’s 2026 lander data is the result to watch, and the tracker lists it. Follow-ups # Simultaneous H₂/O₂ measurements; voltage over time; controls with nodules removed. Microbial versus abiotic partitioning (sterilised incubations).

t: Bell et al. 2025 (Science Advances): How Little We Have Seen
d: The first global estimate of how much of the deep seafloor has ever been imaged: at most 0.001%.
x: How to read this analysis Every analysis follows the same template: citation, access, research question, method, key results, strengths, limitations and critiques, links to the rest of the encyclopedia, an assessment, and follow-ups. Use Open PDF to read a printable copy in a new tab, or Download PDF to save it. Citation: Bell K.L.C., Johannes K.N., Kennedy B.R.C., Poulton S.E. Science Advances 11(19) (7 May 2025). doi:10.1126/sciadv.adp8602 Access: 🔓 Open access Analysis basis: abstract plus the Ocean Discovery League release and coverage. Question # What fraction of the deep seafloor (≥200 m) has ever been directly observed with cameras or human eyes, and where? Method # Compiled a database of ~44,000 deep-sea dives with visual observations since 1958, from public records plus estimates for unreported private dives. Two complementary area estimates: a per-dive footprint by vehicle type, and a track-based method. Key Results # Total area imaged ≈ 2,130–3,823 km² , which is ≤0.001% of the ~336 million km² deep seafloor (roughly a tenth of Belgium). Geographic bias: 65% of observations lie within 200 nmi of the USA, Japan and New Zealand . 97% of dives come from five countries: USA, Japan, NZ, France and Germany. Habitat bias: canyons and ridges are over-sampled. Abyssal plains and seamounts are under-sampled. Only 442 of 9,472 known canyons have ever been seen, and Monterey Canyon alone accounts for ~48% of canyon observations. Even if the estimate were off by 10×, less than 0.01% would have any visual record. Strengths # First quantitative global estimate; transparent about uncertainty. Exposes structural inequity in who explores the ocean. Limitations and Critiques # Private and military dive records are unknown, which is why the authors give an order-of-magnitude buffer. “Seen” doesn’t equal “characterised”. A quick camera pass gives little ecological information. Links to This Hub # ../exploration/exploration-methods-and-records.md and figure seen_vs_mapped_generated.png ../biology/ : why “average deep-sea fauna” claims are risky My Take # This is the most important context number in the hub. Every generalisation about deep-sea life rests on a sample smaller than a mid-size city, drawn mostly from three countries’ waters. It argues for low-cost, distributed exploration tools and for humility in mining impact assessments. Follow-ups # Re-run the estimate in 2030 to test whether new low-cost tools and Ocean Census expeditions bend the curve.

t: Portmann et al. 2026 (Science Advances): AMOC Weakening
d: Observation-constrained projections of a 43–59% AMOC weakening by 2100.
x: How to read this analysis Every analysis follows the same template: citation, access, research question, method, key results, strengths, limitations and critiques, links to the rest of the encyclopedia, an assessment, and follow-ups. Use Open PDF to read a printable copy in a new tab, or Download PDF to save it. Citation: Portmann V., Swingedouw D., Khattab O., Chavent M. Science Advances 12(16) (April 2026). doi:10.1126/sciadv.adx4298 Access: 🔓 Open access Analysis basis: abstract, CNN, Live Science, Science Focus and Science News coverage. Question # Climate models disagree widely on how much the AMOC will weaken by 2100. Can real-world observations narrow that range? Method # Emergent-constraint style approach. It relates each model’s simulated present-day ocean state (temperature and salinity across multiple variables) to its future AMOC change, then uses observations to pick out the most realistic behaviour. Corrects for model collinearity using ridge-regularised linear regression , which is rare in climate science. Key Results # Projected weakening by 2100: ~43–59% (central ~51%). That is about 60% stronger than the unconstrained multi-model mean. Medium to very-high emission scenarios converge on ~50%. Only aggressive, sustained cuts give ~20%. Conclusion: the “pessimistic” high-weakening models are the realistic ones. Strengths # Uses many observed variables at once instead of a single proxy. Substantially reduces uncertainty compared with the raw model spread. Limitations and Critiques # Greenland meltwater is not included in the models, so this may underestimate weakening. It projects weakening, not collapse. The authors stress the distinction, and other experts note results vary widely between studies. Emergent constraints assume the model relationship holds in the future. If shared model biases exist, the constraint inherits them. Links to This Hub # ../ocean-change/ocean-change-2026.md and figure amoc_projection_generated.png My Take # The useful framing is “how much weakening is already baked in versus avoidable”. The difference between ~50% and ~20% is the policy-relevant gap. I’d pair this paper with Holden et al. 2026 (committed-collapse probability) and the observed four-latitude decline to triangulate. Follow-ups # Add a Greenland meltwater forcing sensitivity. Check whether the RAPID 26.5°N array record, about 29 years long by 2033, can separate trend from variability as expected.

Status date: 15 November 2026 . # Stream Status Next milestone 1 ISA Mining Code 31st session ended without the Code; roadmap agreed 32nd session, 2027 2 US deep-sea mining (NOAA/TMC) ~65,000 km² CCZ application fully compliant ; hearing 13 Oct 2026 Certification decision, then EIS 3 High Seas Treaty In force since 17 Jan 2026 ; 86 parties by Mar 2026 COP1 ~Jan 2027 4 Dark oxygen Contested; DORI follow-up launched 2026 lander results 5 Hadal life Chemosynthetic communities to 9,533 m Surveys of other trenches 6 Species discovery 1,121 new species in a year (+54%) Year-4 report ~May 2027 7 Seafloor mapping 28.7% mapped (Apr 2026) Next GEBCO grid ~Jun 2027 8 Visual exploration ≤0.001% ever imaged Low-cost camera programmes 9 Coral bleaching 4th global event (84.4%) ended mid-2025 El Niño risk 2026–27 10 AMOC Weakening observed; 43–59% by 2100 projected RAPID/OSNAP data 1 · ISA Mining Code The International Seabed Authority's 31st session ran in two Council parts (9–19 March and 13–24 July 2026) plus the Assembly (27–31 July). On 24 July the Council agreed a **roadmap** of remaining work but **did not adopt** the exploitation regulations, so no commercial mining has been approved in international waters. **Watch:** the 32nd session (2027) and whether a deadline for the Code is set. **Read more:** [Deep-sea mining](/wiki/impacts/deep-sea-mining.html) · [Who governs the deep?](/wiki/impacts/high-seas-treaty-and-isa.html) **Sources:** [ENB summary](https://enb.iisd.org/international-seabed-authority-isa-council-31-2-summary) · [Benchmark Minerals](https://source.benchmarkminerals.com/article/benchmark-at-the-international-seabed-authority-meeting-as-global-commercial-framework-remained-unresolved) 2 · US deep-sea mining (NOAA / TMC) NOAA's rule combining an exploration licence and commercial recovery permit took effect on 21 January 2026. TMC USA filed for about **65,000 km²** of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone. NOAA found the application **fully compliant** and held a public hearing on **13 October 2026**. TMC says it expects a permit by the end of Q1 2027. **Watch:** NOAA's certification decision, then the Environmental Impact Statement and its comment period. **Sources:** [NOAA](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/noaa-advances-review-of-first-ever-deep-seabed-mining-commercial-recovery-application) · [Barchart](https://www.barchart.com/story/news/1644737/noaa-determines-tmc-usas-consolidated-deep-seabed-mining-application-is-in-full-compliance) 3 · High Seas Treaty (BBNJ) The treaty entered into force on **17 January 2026** and had 86 parties by March. The first Conference of the Parties must meet within a year, and Belgium, Chile and China are bidding to host the secretariat. **Read more:** [Who governs the deep?](/wiki/impacts/high-seas-treaty-and-isa.html) · [Marine protected areas](/wiki/impacts/marine-protected-areas.html) **Sources:** [European Commission](https://oceans-and-fisheries.ec.europa.eu/news/high-seas-treaty-enters-force-milestone-ocean-conservation-2026-01-16_en) · [ELI](https://www.eli.org/vibrant-environment-blog/charting-new-waters-high-seas-treaty-after-two-months) 4 · Dark oxygen The 2024 claim that nodules produce oxygen through seawater electrolysis remains contested. The **Dark Oxygen Research Initiative (DORI)**, a US$5.2M programme, is deploying landers that measure hydrogen and oxygen together. **Read more:** [Sweetman et al. 2024 analysis](/wiki/library/sweetman-2024.html) **Sources:** [SAMS DORI](https://sams.ac.uk/science/projects/dori/) · [Nippon Foundation](https://tnfsa.nippon-foundation.or.jp/news/13238305) 5 · Hadal life *Fendouzhe* dives found chemosynthetic communities over about 2,500 km of the Kuril–Kamchatka and Aleutian trenches, down to **9,533 m**. **Read more:** [Hadal life](/wiki/life/hadal-life.html) · [Peng et al. 2025 analysis](/wiki/library/peng-2025.html) **Source:** doi:10.1038/s41586-025-09317-z · [Nature Asia highlight](https://www.natureasia.com/ja-jp/nature/pr-highlights/15298) 6 · Species discovery (Ocean Census) Year 3 (Apr 2025 – Mar 2026) recorded **1,121** species new to science, 54% above the usual rate. About 728 came through Species Discovery Awards, many from museum backlogs. Formal description usually takes ~13.5 years, which is why the NOVA platform records "discovered" as a status. **Read more:** [Species discovery](/wiki/life/species-discovery.html) **Sources:** [Nekton](https://nektonmission.org/news/scientists-discover-over-1100-new-marine-species-in-landmark-ocean-census/) · [Scientific American](https://scientificamerican.com/article/ocean-census-reveals-more-than-1-100-new-species) 7 · Seafloor mapping (Seabed 2030) **28.7%** of the seafloor was mapped by April 2026, with almost five million km² added in a year. **Read more:** [Mapping the seafloor](/wiki/exploration/mapping-the-seafloor.html) **Source:** [IHO](https://iho.int/en/global-seabed-mapping-reaches-new-milestone-as-five-million-square-kilometres-added-in-a-year) 8 · Visual exploration At most **0.001%** of the deep seafloor has ever been imaged, and 65% of observations lie near the USA, Japan and New Zealand. **Read more:** [How little we have seen](/wiki/exploration/how-little-we-have-seen.html) · [Bell et al. 2025 analysis](/wiki/library/bell-2025.html) 9 · Coral bleaching The fourth global bleaching event reached **84.4%** of reefs (2023–2025). NOAA confirmed its end on 2 June 2026. Researchers describe an era of near-annual bleaching. **Read more:** [Coral bleaching](/wiki/climate/coral-bleaching.html) **Sources:** [NOAA Coral Reef Watch](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/research/coral_bleaching_report.php) · [GCRMN](https://gcrmn.net/2026/06/08/4gbe-ended/) 10 · AMOC Weakening has been observed at four latitudes. Portmann et al. project **43–59% weakening by 2100**, and a July 2026 study argues collapse may alread

d: Run the physics yourself: dive to any depth and watch pressure, light and temperature change in real time.
x: Dive Profile Lab # Drag the submersible from the surface to the bottom of the Challenger Deep. The lab shows pressure (atmospheres and kg per cm²), remaining sunlight , typical temperature , the ocean zone , and which animals and vehicles live or operate at that depth. ▶ Open the Dive Profile Lab in a new tab The physics behind it # Pressure: about 1 atm plus 1 atm for every 10 m. That is roughly 1,090 atm at the Challenger Deep. See Pressure, light and temperature . Light: decays roughly exponentially. In clear ocean about 1% remains near 100 m, and effectively none below 1,000 m. Temperature: a warm mixed layer, then the thermocline, then 0–4 °C almost everywhere below ~1,000 m.

d: Neither squid nor octopus: a gentle detritus eater living in the oxygen minimum zone.
x: Overview # The sole surviving member of its order. Despite its name it is not predatory: it collects marine snow with two retractile filaments and mucus. Habitat and type of water # Tropical and temperate oceans in oxygen minimum zones, 600–1,200 m. Feeding and hunting # Gathers sinking organic particles with sticky filaments and rolls them into mucus balls to eat. Mating and reproduction # Unusually for cephalopods, it appears to spawn multiple times over its life, with resting phases between. Movement and migration # Stays within the oxygen minimum zone, where few predators can follow. Behaviour and social life # When threatened it turns its webbed cloak inside out (‘pineapple posture’) and ejects glowing mucus instead of ink. Feeding and hunting # A sit-and-wait ambush predator. It hangs motionless and wiggles its glowing lure to draw prey close, then engulfs it. Its stomach and jaws expand so it can swallow prey as large as itself, which matters where meals are rare. Mating and reproduction # Males are tiny and free-swimming, with large nostrils for tracking female pheromones. In Melanocetus the male attaches temporarily to the female; in some other anglerfish families males fuse permanently (sexual parasitism). Eggs are released in buoyant gelatinous veils, and larvae develop in shallower water. Movement and migration # Larvae and juveniles live higher in the water column and descend as they mature (ontogenetic migration). Adults do not migrate daily. Behaviour and social life # Solitary, energy-saving and largely motionless. Encounters between the sexes are rare, which is why mate-finding adaptations are so extreme. Adaptations # Bacterial bioluminescent lure Distensible stomach and hinged jaws Black, light-absorbing skin Weak, watery muscles that save energy Conservation # Not commercially fished. The main threats are indirect (deep-sea trawling bycatch, climate-driven changes in food supply). d: Possibly the most abundant vertebrates on Earth; their nightly migration is the largest on the planet.
x: Overview # About 250 species of small fish covered in photophores (light organs) in species-specific patterns. Together they may make up a large share of the global fish biomass, and they underpin food webs for tuna, squid, seabirds and marine mammals. Habitat and type of water # Every ocean, mesopelagic zone by day (300–1,500 m), near-surface by night. Feeding and hunting # Feed at night near the surface on copepods, krill and other zooplankton, then descend at dawn to digest in dark, cold water safe from visual predators. Mating and reproduction # Broadcast spawners with pelagic eggs and larvae. Many species mature within a year, and their short lives support rapid population turnover. Movement and migration # Diel vertical migration: hundreds of metres up at dusk and down at dawn, every day. This transports carbon to depth (the ‘migrant pump’). Behaviour and social life # Schooling. Photophores on the belly provide counter-illumination, matching downwelling light to hide the fish’s silhouette from predators below. Adaptations # Ventral photophores for counter-illumination Large eyes tuned to blue light Gas-filled or lipid-filled swim bladders (varies by species) Conservation # Targeted by small experimental fisheries for fishmeal. Scientists caution that large-scale twilight-zone fishing could weaken the ocean’s carbon pump. d: A slow-growing deep-sea fish that can live past 150 years; its fishery became a cautionary tale.
x: Overview # Orange roughy aggregate around seamounts and steep slopes. They mature very late (20–30+ years), so populations recover slowly from fishing. Habitat and type of water # Cold deep waters of the Atlantic, Indo-Pacific and especially around New Zealand and Australia, often over seamounts. Feeding and hunting # Feeds on mesopelagic prey drawn to seamounts by currents. Mating and reproduction # Forms dense spawning aggregations, which made it easy to catch in very large quantities. Fecundity is low for its size. Movement and migration # Moves between feeding and spawning grounds on seamounts. Behaviour and social life # Aggregates in large schools around seamounts. Adaptations # Extremely slow metabolism and growth Long lifespan Conservation # Many stocks were heavily overfished in the 1980s–90s. Bottom trawling on seamounts also destroyed coral habitat. d: A 'living fossil' lobe-finned fish thought extinct for 66 million years until found off South Africa in 1938.
x: Overview # Coelacanths belong to an ancient lineage more closely related to tetrapods than most fish are. Their fleshy lobed fins move in a pattern similar to the alternating gait of four-legged animals. Habitat and type of water # Volcanic slopes and caves off the Comoros, Mozambique, Madagascar, South Africa and Tanzania, typically 100–500 m. A second species lives in Indonesia. Feeding and hunting # Drifts head-down near reefs at night hunting fish and squid, using an electroreceptive rostral organ. Mating and reproduction # Ovoviviparous: eggs hatch inside the mother and she gives birth to live young after a gestation estimated at about 5 years, one of the longest known in vertebrates. Movement and migration # Rests in caves by day and drifts on currents to forage at night. Behaviour and social life # Gathers peacefully in caves by day. Individuals are recognisable by their spot patterns. Adaptations # Lobed, limb-like fins Rostral electroreceptor Fat-filled vestigial lung Conservation # Very small population, threatened by bycatch in deep-set shark nets. d: The largest and deepest ocean, covering about a third of Earth's surface.
x: Overview # The Pacific is the largest single feature on Earth’s surface: at about 165 million km² it is bigger than all the land combined and holds roughly half of the planet’s free water. It stretches about 15,500 km from the Bering Strait to Antarctica and nearly 20,000 km from Indonesia to Colombia. Its name, ‘peaceful sea’, came from Magellan in 1520, but it is the most geologically violent ocean, ringed by the Ring of Fire. Its tropical belt generates the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the most important source of year-to-year climate variability on the planet. Geography # Bounded by Asia and Australia to the west, the Americas to the east and the Southern Ocean to the south (about 60°S). Marginal seas include the Bering, Okhotsk, Japan, Yellow, East and South China, Philippine, Coral and Tasman seas. More than 25,000 islands lie in the Pacific, more than in all other oceans combined, grouped into Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia. Seafloor and geology # The Pacific plate is the largest tectonic plate and is being consumed at subduction zones on almost every side. That creates the deepest trenches on Earth: Mariana (Challenger Deep, ~10,935 m), Tonga (~10,800 m), Philippine, Kuril–Kamchatka, Kermadec and Japan trenches. The East Pacific Rise spreads up to ~15 cm a year, the fastest on Earth, and hosts black-smoker vents. Tens of thousands of seamounts and guyots dot the basin, including the Hawaiian–Emperor chain that records the plate’s motion over a hotspot. The Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico holds the world’s richest polymetallic nodule fields. Water and currents # Two great gyres (North and South Pacific) circulate clockwise and anticlockwise. The Kuroshio is the Pacific’s Gulf Stream; the California and Humboldt currents carry cold water toward the equator and drive rich upwelling. The tropical Pacific warm pool is the warmest large body of ocean water. Every 2–7 years El Niño weakens the trade winds and warms the eastern Pacific, while La Niña does the opposite; the swings shift rainfall, cyclones and fisheries worldwide. The eastern tropical Pacific holds the largest oxygen minimum zone in the ocean. Climate, weather and cyclones # The western North Pacific produces more tropical cyclones (typhoons) than any other basin, about a third of the global total, including the strongest storms on record. El Niño years bring floods to Peru, drought to Australia and Indonesia, and weaker Indian monsoons. The Pacific Decadal Oscillation shifts sea temperatures over decades, and the 2014–16 ‘Blob’ marine heatwave killed seabirds, whales and kelp along North America. Flora and fauna # The Coral Triangle (Indonesia, Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands) holds about 76% of all known coral species and the world’s richest reef fish diversity. The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on Earth. Kelp forests line California and Chile. Upwelling off Pe

d: The second-largest ocean, split down the middle by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and home to the AMOC.
x: Overview # The Atlantic is the second-largest ocean (about 106 million km²) and the youngest of the major basins, opening as Pangaea broke apart around 180 million years ago. It is still widening by about 2.5 cm a year along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. It is the saltiest open ocean and the engine room of the global overturning circulation: cold, salty water sinks in the north and spreads through the deep ocean worldwide. That makes the Atlantic central to Earth’s climate. Geography # An S-shaped basin between the Americas to the west and Europe and Africa to the east, from the Arctic to the Southern Ocean. Marginal seas include the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Mediterranean, North, Baltic, Norwegian and Labrador seas, plus the Sargasso Sea, the only sea with no coastline. It drains more river water than any other ocean, including the Amazon, Congo, Mississippi and Niger. Seafloor and geology # The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs ~16,000 km down the centre and rises above sea level in Iceland and the Azores. Vent fields such as TAG, Rainbow and the alkaline Lost City lie along it. The deepest point is the Milwaukee Deep in the Puerto Rico Trench (~8,376 m); the South Sandwich Trench lies in the far south. Wide continental shelves (Grand Banks, North Sea, Patagonian shelf) host rich fisheries, and submarine canyons cut the margins. Water and currents # The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Current carry tropical heat to Europe. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) sinks water in the Labrador and Nordic seas, forming North Atlantic Deep Water. In the south, the Benguela upwelling off Namibia is one of the most productive systems on Earth. Salinity reaches ~37 PSU in the subtropics because evaporation exceeds rainfall. Climate, weather and cyclones # The tropical Atlantic produces hurricanes from June to November, born from African easterly waves over warm water above ~26.5°C. The North Atlantic Oscillation steers European winters. A weakening AMOC is one of the major climate tipping-point concerns (see AMOC weakening). Flora and fauna # Cold-water coral reefs off Norway and Ireland, the cod and herring stocks of the Grand Banks and North Sea, North Atlantic right whales, humpbacks breeding in the Caribbean, Atlantic bluefin tuna crossing the basin, the Sargasso Sea’s floating sargassum community where European and American eels spawn, sea turtles, gannets, puffins, and the Lost City vent fauna. Ecosystems # Sargassum mats, coral reefs (Caribbean), cold-water coral mounds, seagrass and mangroves, upwelling systems (Benguela, Canary), vent and seep communities, and the abyssal plains of the Cape Verde and Sohm basins. History and exploration # Vikings reached North America around 1000 CE; Columbus crossed in 1492. The Atlantic slave trade forcibly carried over 12 million Africans across it. Matthew Maury charted its winds and currents in the 1850s; the first transatlantic telegraph cable was laid in 1858. Famous wrecks include the Titani

d: The warmest ocean, ruled by monsoon reversals of winds and currents.
x: Overview # The Indian Ocean (~70.5 million km²) is the third-largest and the warmest ocean. Unlike the Pacific and Atlantic, it is closed to the north by Asia, so it has no northern polar water. Instead its circulation is ruled by the monsoon: winds and major currents reverse direction twice a year. It is named after India, whose rainfall, agriculture and economy depend directly on its behaviour. Geography # Bounded by Africa to the west, Asia to the north, Australia and Indonesia to the east and the Southern Ocean to the south. Marginal seas include the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, Andaman Sea, Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Laccadive Sea and Mozambique Channel. Island groups include Madagascar, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Lakshadweep, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Seychelles, Mauritius and Réunion. Major rivers include the Ganges–Brahmaputra, Indus, Zambezi and Irrawaddy. Seafloor and geology # The Java (Sunda) Trench (~7,290 m) is its deepest point and the source of the 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake and tsunami. Three ridges (Central, Southwest and Southeast Indian ridges) meet at the Rodrigues Triple Junction, where the Kairei vent field hosts the scaly-foot snail. The Bengal Fan, built by sediment from the Himalaya via the Ganges–Brahmaputra, is the largest submarine fan on Earth. The Central Indian Ocean Basin holds nodule fields explored by India under an ISA contract. Water and currents # During the southwest monsoon (June–September) the Somali Current flows north at up to ~3.5 m/s and drives strong upwelling off Somalia, Oman and western India; in the northeast monsoon it reverses. The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), a see-saw of temperatures between west and east, shapes rainfall in India, East Africa and Australia. The Agulhas Current, one of the strongest western boundary currents, leaks warm salty water into the Atlantic. The Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal hold intense oxygen minimum zones. Climate, weather and cyclones # The Bay of Bengal produces some of the deadliest tropical cyclones in history, because a shallow, funnel-shaped bay amplifies storm surges onto the low Ganges delta. Arabian Sea cyclones have become more frequent and intense as it warms. Monsoon rain from the ocean supplies most of India’s annual rainfall. The Indian Ocean is warming faster than any other ocean, intensifying marine heatwaves. Flora and fauna # Coelacanths off South Africa and Comoros, whale sharks of the Maldives and Ningaloo, dugongs, olive ridley turtles mass-nesting in Odisha, the Sundarbans mangroves with their tigers and Ganges river dolphins, manta rays of the Maldives, hilsa migrating up the Bengal rivers, and vent fauna like the scaly-foot snail. Ecosystems # Coral atolls (Maldives, Lakshadweep, Chagos), the Sundarbans (the world’s largest mangrove forest), seagrass meadows grazed by dugongs, upwelling systems, deep oxygen minimum zones and hydrothermal vents. History and exploration # Monsoon winds powered trade between Africa, Arabia, Indi

d: The ring of ocean around Antarctica, driven by the strongest current on Earth.
x: Overview # The Southern Ocean encircles Antarctica south of about 60°S and was formally recognised as the fifth ocean by the International Hydrographic Organization in 2000 (and by National Geographic in 2021). It is defined less by coastlines than by a current: the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the largest current on Earth. It is the ocean’s main gateway between surface and deep water, absorbing a large share of the heat and carbon dioxide that humans add to the climate system. Geography # Surrounds Antarctica, with the Weddell, Ross, Amundsen, Bellingshausen and Scotia seas as major embayments. The Drake Passage between South America and the Antarctic Peninsula is its narrowest point. Sub-Antarctic islands such as South Georgia, Kerguelen, Heard and Macquarie are wildlife strongholds. Seafloor and geology # The South Sandwich Trench (~7,400 m, the Factorian Deep) is the deepest point. Continental shelves around Antarctica are unusually deep (~500 m) because the weight of the ice sheet pushes the crust down. Mid-ocean ridges and seamounts steer the circumpolar current. Water and currents # The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows eastward around the continent, carrying over 100 times the flow of all the world’s rivers. Antarctic Bottom Water, the densest water in the ocean, forms on the Weddell and Ross shelves as sea ice forms and rejects salt, then spreads along the floor of all oceans. Upwelling of old deep water around Antarctica brings nutrients and CO₂ back to the surface. Climate, weather and cyclones # Westerly winds are the strongest on Earth (‘Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Screaming Sixties’). Sea ice expands each winter to about 18 million km² and shrinks to ~3 million km² in summer; record lows since 2016, and especially 2023, have alarmed scientists. Warm water reaching beneath ice shelves (Thwaites, Pine Island) threatens future sea-level rise. Flora and fauna # Antarctic krill (perhaps the largest biomass of any wild animal species), emperor, Adélie, chinstrap, gentoo and king penguins, Weddell, leopard and crabeater seals, blue, humpback, fin and minke whales, albatrosses and petrels, and icefish with no red blood cells. Benthic communities include giant sea spiders and slow-growing sponges. Ecosystems # Sea-ice ecosystems (algae under ice), krill-based food webs, sub-Antarctic island seabird and seal colonies, deep continental shelves, and the ice-shelf cavities beneath floating ice. History and exploration # Cook crossed the Antarctic Circle in 1773. Sealers and whalers devastated fur seals and great whales in the 19th and 20th centuries. The Antarctic Treaty (1959) set the continent aside for peace and science; CCAMLR (1982) manages its marine life. Shackleton’s Endurance sank in the Weddell Sea in 1915 and was found at 3,008 m in 2022. People and economy # Krill and toothfish fisheries regulated by CCAMLR; tourism to the Antarctic Peninsula; research stations from about 30 nations, including

d: The smallest, shallowest ocean, losing its summer sea ice fast.
x: Overview # The Arctic is the smallest (~15.6 million km²) and shallowest ocean, mostly enclosed by Eurasia and North America. Much of it is covered by sea ice that grows and shrinks with the seasons. It is warming about four times faster than the global average, so its ice cover is one of the clearest signals of climate change. Geography # Ringed by Russia, Norway, Greenland, Canada and Alaska. Marginal seas include the Barents, Kara, Laptev, East Siberian, Chukchi and Beaufort seas, plus Baffin Bay and Hudson Bay. The Fram Strait is the main deep connection to the Atlantic; the narrow Bering Strait links it to the Pacific. Seafloor and geology # The Arctic has the widest continental shelves on Earth, especially off Siberia, holding about half its area. The Lomonosov Ridge divides it into the Amerasian and Eurasian basins; the Gakkel Ridge is the slowest-spreading ridge on Earth yet hosts active vents (the Aurora field). The deepest point is the Molloy Deep (~5,550 m) in the Fram Strait. Water and currents # The Beaufort Gyre stores fresh water from rivers and melting ice, and the Transpolar Drift carries ice from Siberia toward Fram Strait. Huge Siberian rivers (Ob, Yenisei, Lena) make the surface fresher than any other ocean. Atlantic water entering through the Barents Sea is warming the Arctic from below (‘Atlantification’). Climate, weather and cyclones # September sea-ice extent has fallen by about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979, and multi-year ice has largely disappeared. Loss of white ice exposes dark water that absorbs more sunlight, accelerating warming (ice–albedo feedback). Thawing subsea permafrost may release methane. Flora and fauna # Polar bears, walruses, ringed and bearded seals, narwhals, belugas and bowhead whales, polar cod living in ice cracks, ice algae, Arctic char, little auks and ivory gulls. The Bering and Barents seas host some of the richest fisheries on Earth. Ecosystems # Sea-ice ecosystems, polynyas (open-water oases in ice), shallow Siberian shelves, the Barents Sea cod system and vents on the Gakkel Ridge. History and exploration # Inuit and other Indigenous peoples have lived along its coasts for millennia. Searches for the Northwest Passage killed Franklin’s 1845 expedition; its ships Erebus and Terror were found in 2014 and 2016. Nansen’s Fram drifted across it in 1893–96; the submarine USS Nautilus passed under the North Pole in 1958. People and economy # Indigenous subsistence hunting, Barents Sea and Bering Sea fisheries, Arctic shipping routes opening as ice melts (the Northern Sea Route), and oil and gas exploration. Threats and protection # Rapid ice loss, Atlantification, shipping and oil-spill risk, microplastics trapped in sea ice, and fisheries moving north into unregulated waters (a central Arctic fishing moratorium was agreed in 2018). Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer

d: A nearly enclosed sea with unusually warm, salty deep water and a long human history.
x: Overview # Connected to the Atlantic by the 14 km-wide Strait of Gibraltar. It nearly dried out during the Messinian salinity crisis (~5.9–5.3 million years ago). Geography # Between Europe, North Africa and Western Asia. Seafloor and geology # A complex basin of sub-basins (Alboran, Tyrrhenian, Ionian, Aegean, Levantine) with the Calypso Deep (~5,267 m) off Greece. About 5.6 million years ago it nearly dried out in the Messinian Salinity Crisis, leaving thick salt layers; the Zanclean flood through Gibraltar refilled it. Brine pools and mud volcanoes lie on its floor. Water and currents # Evaporation exceeds inflow, so it is very salty. Deep water stays ~13 °C, much warmer than most of the deep ocean. Climate, weather and cyclones # A hot, dry-summer ‘Mediterranean climate’. It is warming ~20% faster than the global ocean, with repeated marine heatwaves since 2003 causing mass die-offs of gorgonians and the noble pen shell. ‘Medicanes’ (Mediterranean hurricane-like storms) such as Daniel in 2023 caused catastrophic floods in Libya. Flora and fauna # Posidonia seagrass meadows, monk seals, bluefin tuna spawning grounds. A biodiversity hotspot with many endemics. Ecosystems # Posidonia seagrass meadows, coralligenous reefs, red coral, submarine caves, deep cold-water corals, and over 1,000 non-native species that arrived through the Suez Canal (Lessepsian migration). History and exploration # Cradle of Phoenician, Greek and Roman sea trade. Wrecks include the Antikythera wreck (with the Antikythera mechanism, the oldest known analogue computer) and Bronze Age ships like Uluburun. Jacques Cousteau pioneered scuba diving here. People and economy # Over 150 million coastal inhabitants and heavy tourism. Threats and protection # Marine heatwaves, invasive species via the Suez Canal, overfishing, plastics. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Mediterranean%20Sea

d: A tropical sea of coral reefs and the deepest point of the Caribbean, the Cayman Trough.
x: Overview # Bounded by the Antilles island arcs and Central/South America. Geography # Contains the Mesoamerican Reef, the second-largest barrier reef system. Seafloor and geology # Floored by the Caribbean plate, with the Cayman Trough (~7,686 m) and the Mid-Cayman Rise, home to the deepest known black smokers (Beebe vent field, ~5,000 m). The Puerto Rico Trench lies just to the north. Water and currents # Warm surface waters fuel Atlantic hurricanes. Climate, weather and cyclones # The core of the Atlantic hurricane belt: warm water (>26.5°C) fuels storms from June to November. Sargassum influxes since 2011 smother beaches. Repeated heatwaves have bleached most reefs. Flora and fauna # Reef fish, sea turtles, invasive lionfish, the world’s deepest known vents (Beebe vent field, ~5,000 m). Ecosystems # Coral reefs, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef (second-largest reef system), mangroves, seagrass with manatees and turtles, and deep vents. History and exploration # Columbus arrived in 1492; the Spanish treasure fleets and pirates of the 17th–18th centuries left many wrecks, including the San José galleon (found off Colombia in 2015). People and economy # Tourism and fisheries economies. Threats and protection # Bleaching, Sargassum influxes, invasive lionfish. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Caribbean%20Sea

d: A basin of natural oil seeps, brine pools and a large seasonal 'dead zone'.
x: Overview # Partly enclosed by the US, Mexico and Cuba. Geography # Fed by the Loop Current and the Mississippi River. Seafloor and geology # Wide shelves around a deep central basin (Sigsbee Deep, ~4,384 m). Salt domes and cold seeps produce brine pools and methane hydrates; the Chicxulub crater from the dinosaur-killing asteroid lies under its southern rim. Water and currents # Nutrient runoff from the Mississippi creates a large hypoxic zone each summer. Climate, weather and cyclones # The Loop Current feeds warm water that intensifies hurricanes (Katrina 2005, Harvey 2017, Ian 2022). Mississippi River nutrients create a summer ‘dead zone’ of hypoxic water averaging ~14,000 km². Flora and fauna # Brine pools with ‘hot tub of despair’ lakes, cold seeps, giant isopods. Ecosystems # Seagrass, oyster reefs, the Flower Garden Banks coral reefs, cold seeps with tubeworms and ice worms, and Kemp’s ridley turtle nesting beaches. History and exploration # The 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill released ~4.9 million barrels of oil, the largest marine spill in US history. People and economy # Major oil and gas region. Deepwater Horizon spill in 2010. Threats and protection # Hypoxia, oil pollution, intensifying hurricanes. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Gulf%20of%20Mexico

d: The only sea without coastlines, defined by currents and floating Sargassum seaweed.
x: Overview # Bounded by the currents of the North Atlantic Gyre. Geography # Mid-North Atlantic around Bermuda. Seafloor and geology # Overlies deep abyssal plains (Nares and Hatteras) and the Bermuda Rise; about 4,500–6,500 m deep. Water and currents # Calm, clear and warm. Sargassum mats float at the surface. Climate, weather and cyclones # Bounded only by currents of the North Atlantic Gyre, so it has calm, clear, nutrient-poor warm water. The Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study (since 1988) records ocean warming and acidification here. Flora and fauna # The spawning ground of European and American eels, and a nursery for turtles. Ecosystems # Floating sargassum mats host endemic sargassum fish, crabs and nudibranchs, and nurseries for sea turtles. It is the spawning ground of European and American eels. History and exploration # Named by Portuguese sailors; Columbus feared his ships would be trapped in its weed. The 2014 Hamilton Declaration created a commission for its conservation. People and economy # Hamilton Declaration (2014) for conservation cooperation. Threats and protection # Plastic accumulation in the gyre, shipping. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Sargasso%20Sea

d: A shallow, heavily used shelf sea between Britain and mainland Europe.
x: Overview # Formed over a drowned landscape (Doggerland) flooded after the last ice age. Geography # Between the UK, Norway, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Seafloor and geology # A shallow shelf sea (average ~95 m) that was dry land, Doggerland, until about 8,000 years ago; fishermen still trawl up mammoth bones and Stone Age tools. The Norwegian Trench reaches ~700 m. Water and currents # Shallow and well-mixed, with strong tides. Climate, weather and cyclones # Severe winter storms and storm surges (the 1953 flood killed over 2,000 people in the Netherlands and UK). Warming has shifted cod north and brought in warm-water species. Flora and fauna # Herring, cod, harbour porpoises, grey seals. Ecosystems # Sandbanks, oyster reefs (being restored), Wadden Sea mudflats (a UNESCO World Heritage site), seal colonies and seabird cliffs. History and exploration # Viking routes, the Hanseatic League, the Battle of Jutland (1916) whose wrecks lie on the floor, North Sea oil since 1970 and now the world’s largest offshore wind farms. People and economy # Oil and gas, the largest offshore wind build-out in the world, shipping. Threats and protection # Bottom trawling (high carbon disturbance), heavy shipping. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=North%20Sea

d: A young brackish sea with some of the largest dead zones on Earth.
x: Overview # Formed after the last glaciation and still rising due to post-glacial rebound. Geography # Enclosed by Scandinavia, the Baltic states, Poland, Germany, Russia and Finland. Seafloor and geology # A young, shallow (average ~55 m) brackish sea left by the retreating ice sheet; the Landsort Deep reaches ~459 m. Land is still rising after the ice age. Water and currents # A low-salinity surface over a salty, often anoxic deep layer. Climate, weather and cyclones # Very low salinity (from ~2 PSU in the north to ~20 at the entrance) and limited exchange with the North Sea make it vulnerable. Its deep basins have one of the world’s largest dead zones, caused by nutrient runoff. Flora and fauna # Few species tolerate brackish water. Grey seals, cod (in decline). Ecosystems # A mix of marine and freshwater species, bladderwrack, grey and ringed seals, harbour porpoises, cod and herring. History and exploration # The cold, low-salinity water lacks shipworms, so wrecks survive intact, from the Swedish warship Vasa (1628, raised in 1961) to medieval cogs. People and economy # Shipping and fishing. Threats and protection # Eutrophication and hypoxia, overfishing. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Baltic%20Sea

d: The largest anoxic body of water on Earth: below ~150–200 m there is no oxygen.
x: Overview # A meromictic sea: the layers never mix fully. Geography # Between Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Anatolia, linked to the Mediterranean through the Bosporus. Seafloor and geology # A deep basin (~2,212 m) linked to the Mediterranean only by the narrow Bosporus. Below ~150 m the water has no oxygen and is full of hydrogen sulfide, the largest anoxic water body on Earth. Water and currents # Hydrogen-sulfide-rich deep water preserves ancient shipwrecks remarkably well. Climate, weather and cyclones # Strong stratification: a fresher surface layer from rivers (Danube, Dnieper, Don) sits above dense salty water that never mixes. Flora and fauna # Life mostly confined to the upper ~150 m. Dolphins, anchovy. Ecosystems # Surface life includes dolphins, anchovy and turbot; the sulfidic depths hold only microbes. The invasive comb jelly Mnemiopsis collapsed fisheries in the 1980s. History and exploration # Because there is no oxygen, wooden shipwrecks are perfectly preserved: the 2018 Black Sea MAP project found a Greek trading ship ~2,400 years old, the oldest intact shipwreck known. People and economy # Fisheries and strategic shipping. Threats and protection # Eutrophication, invasive comb jellies (historic), conflict. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Black%20Sea

d: A young ocean in the making, with heat-tolerant corals and hot brine pools.
x: Overview # Africa and Arabia are rifting apart here. Geography # Between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula; connected to the Indian Ocean (Bab-el-Mandeb) and the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal. Seafloor and geology # A young ocean in the making, formed as Africa and Arabia split apart; the central rift reaches ~3,040 m and holds hot brine pools such as Atlantis II Deep. Water and currents # Very salty and warm. Deep water stays ~21 °C. Climate, weather and cyclones # Among the warmest and saltiest seas (~40 PSU) because of extreme evaporation and almost no rivers. Its northern corals are unusually heat-tolerant and may be a refuge as oceans warm. Flora and fauna # Corals unusually tolerant of heat, brine-pool microbes. Ecosystems # Fringing coral reefs with high endemism, whale sharks, dugongs and Red Sea clownfish. History and exploration # A trade route since antiquity; the Suez Canal (1869) connected it to the Mediterranean. People and economy # One of the busiest shipping routes (Suez). Threats and protection # Coastal development, shipping disruption. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Red%20Sea

d: Home to one of the world's thickest oxygen minimum zones, driven by monsoon upwelling.
x: Overview # Bounded by India, Pakistan, Iran and the Arabian Peninsula. Geography # North-western Indian Ocean. Seafloor and geology # Includes the Carlsberg Ridge and the Indus Fan, the second-largest submarine fan. Water and currents # Summer monsoon upwelling drives huge productivity and a deep oxygen minimum zone. Climate, weather and cyclones # The southwest monsoon drives intense upwelling and plankton blooms. It holds one of the world’s thickest oxygen minimum zones, and cyclones have become more frequent as it warms (e.g. Tauktae 2021 and Biparjoy 2023). Flora and fauna # Lanternfish swarms, whale sharks, the Arabian humpback whale (a resident, isolated population). Ecosystems # Upwelling-driven fisheries (oil sardine, mackerel), Lakshadweep atolls and the Gulf of Kutch coral reefs. History and exploration # Ancient Harappan ports such as Lothal and Indo-Roman trade; Mumbai and Karachi are major ports. People and economy # Fisheries and shipping to the Gulf. Threats and protection # Expanding low-oxygen zones, cyclones intensified by warming. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Arabian%20Sea

d: The world's largest bay, freshened by the Ganges–Brahmaputra and fuelling strong cyclones.
x: Overview # Receives enormous river discharge and sediment (the Bengal Fan, the largest submarine fan). Geography # Bounded by India, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. Seafloor and geology # Floored by the Bengal Fan, the largest submarine fan on Earth, built from Himalayan sediment carried by the Ganges and Brahmaputra. Water and currents # A freshwater lid causes strong stratification, which favours cyclone intensification. Climate, weather and cyclones # Huge river inflow makes the surface fresh and strongly stratified, keeping it warm and favouring intense cyclones. Its funnel shape and low coasts amplify storm surges (Bhola 1970, Odisha super cyclone 1999, Amphan 2020). Flora and fauna # Mangrove Sundarbans, Irrawaddy dolphins, olive ridley turtle mass nesting (arribadas in Odisha). Ecosystems # The Sundarbans mangroves, olive ridley mass-nesting in Odisha, hilsa runs, Irrawaddy dolphins and the Andaman reefs. History and exploration # Chola kingdom naval expeditions; Kolkata, Chennai, Visakhapatnam and Chittagong are major ports. People and economy # Dense coastal populations and fisheries. Threats and protection # Cyclones, sea-level rise, oxygen minimum zone. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Bay%20of%20Bengal

d: Home to the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system on Earth.
x: Overview # Off north-east Australia. Geography # Between Australia, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu. Seafloor and geology # Holds the Great Barrier Reef on its western margin and deep basins over ~9,000 m in the New Hebrides Trench nearby. Water and currents # Warm tropical waters. Climate, weather and cyclones # Cyclone-prone in the austral summer; repeated mass bleaching since 1998 (2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024). Flora and fauna # The Great Barrier Reef (~2,300 km). The Ocean Census found many new species here in 2025–26. Ecosystems # The Great Barrier Reef, the world’s largest reef system, with ~1,500 fish species, dugongs, nesting turtles and Osprey Reef sharks. History and exploration # The 1942 Battle of the Coral Sea was the first naval battle fought entirely by aircraft carriers. People and economy # Tourism and a protected marine park. Threats and protection # Repeated mass bleaching (2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024). Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Coral%20Sea

d: A biodiverse and contested sea crossed by a large share of global shipping.
x: Overview # Bounded by China, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. Geography # Western Pacific marginal sea. Seafloor and geology # Shelves in the north and south around a deep central basin (~5,500 m); the Spratly and Paracel reefs. Water and currents # Monsoon-driven circulation. Climate, weather and cyclones # Typhoon-prone; driven by the East Asian monsoon. Flora and fauna # Extensive reefs (Spratlys, Paracels) and large fisheries. Ecosystems # Coral reefs at the edge of the Coral Triangle, seagrass, and some of the world’s most heavily fished waters. History and exploration # Maritime Silk Road trade; today about a third of global shipping passes through, and overlapping territorial claims make it a geopolitical flashpoint. People and economy # A major trade route. Threats and protection # Reef destruction by island building, overfishing, territorial disputes. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=South%20China%20Sea

d: A semi-enclosed sea that forms its own deep water, like a mini-ocean.
x: Overview # Enclosed by Japan, Korea and Russia. Geography # Western Pacific. Seafloor and geology # A nearly enclosed back-arc basin (~3,742 m) whose straits are shallow, so it has its own deep water mass. Water and currents # Forms its own deep water in winter, which is weakening with warming. Climate, weather and cyclones # Cold winter monsoon winds form deep water locally; this formation has weakened with warming. Flora and fauna # Squid fisheries, Japanese spider crabs nearby. Ecosystems # Snow crabs, firefly squid (Toyama Bay), Japanese flying squid and Pacific saury. History and exploration # The 1905 Battle of Tsushima. The sea’s name is disputed (Korea uses ‘East Sea’). People and economy # Fisheries. Threats and protection # Warming, ventilation decline. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Japan Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Sea%20of%20Japan%20(East%20Sea)

d: One of the most productive seas on Earth, supporting huge pollock and crab fisheries.
x: Overview # Between Alaska and Russia, connecting to the Arctic via the Bering Strait. Geography # North Pacific. Seafloor and geology # A broad shallow shelf in the east (the drowned Bering land bridge, Beringia) and a deep basin in the west. Water and currents # Seasonal sea ice drives a rich spring bloom. Climate, weather and cyclones # Seasonal sea ice drives the ecosystem; the 2018–19 ice-free winters and heatwave triggered the collapse of the snow crab fishery. Flora and fauna # Walrus, fur seals, king crab, pollock. Ecosystems # Walrus, Steller sea lions, northern fur seals, seabirds in millions, and the pollock and king crab fisheries. History and exploration # People crossed Beringia into the Americas; Vitus Bering explored it in 1728 and 1741. People and economy # A major share of US seafood landings. Threats and protection # Sea-ice loss leading to crab population crashes (2021–22). Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bering_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Bering%20Sea

d: A major source of Antarctic Bottom Water and the resting place of Shackleton's Endurance.
x: Overview # Off the Antarctic Peninsula and Coats Land. Geography # Southern Ocean. Seafloor and geology # Deep shelf and abyssal plain; the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf covers its southern part. Water and currents # Brine rejection from sea ice forms some of the densest water on Earth. Climate, weather and cyclones # The main source of Antarctic Bottom Water. Its clockwise gyre traps thick sea ice. Flora and fauna # Icefish nesting colonies (~60 million nests found in 2021), emperor penguins. Ecosystems # Emperor penguin colonies, Weddell seals and, in 2021, a vast colony of ~60 million nesting icefish found on the seabed. History and exploration # Shackleton’s Endurance was crushed by its ice in 1915 and found at 3,008 m in 2022. People and economy # A proposed marine protected area. Threats and protection # Sea-ice change. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weddell_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Weddell%20Sea

d: Often called the most pristine marine ecosystem left, and protected by a large MPA since 2017.
x: Overview # A deep bay of the Southern Ocean beside the Ross Ice Shelf. Geography # Antarctica. Seafloor and geology # Contains the Ross Ice Shelf, the largest floating ice shelf (about the size of France). Water and currents # Polynyas drive high productivity. Climate, weather and cyclones # Polynyas produce sea ice and dense water; considered one of the least altered ocean ecosystems. Flora and fauna # Antarctic toothfish, Adélie and emperor penguins, Weddell seals. Ecosystems # Antarctic toothfish, Adélie and emperor penguins, Ross Sea orcas and Weddell seals. History and exploration # Ross discovered it in 1841. The Ross Sea MPA (2016) was the first large high-seas MPA, about 1.55 million km². People and economy # Ross Sea region MPA (~1.55 million km²). Threats and protection # Toothfish fishing pressure, warming. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Ross%20Sea

d: A hot, hyper-saline shallow sea whose corals survive extremes that kill corals elsewhere.
x: Overview # Between the Arabian Peninsula and Iran. Geography # Indian Ocean (via the Strait of Hormuz). Seafloor and geology # Shallow (average ~35 m), formed as a foreland basin of the Zagros mountains; dry land during the last ice age. Water and currents # Summer surface temperatures above 35 °C. Climate, weather and cyclones # Some of the hottest seawater on Earth (over 35°C in summer) and very salty; its corals tolerate heat that would kill others. Flora and fauna # Heat-tolerant corals, dugongs. Ecosystems # Corals, dugongs, seagrass and pearl oysters. History and exploration # Pearl diving was the economic base of the Gulf for millennia before oil. People and economy # Oil and gas, desalination. Threats and protection # Brine discharge, heat extremes. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Persian%20Gulf

d: Between Australia and New Zealand, a marine-heatwave hotspot.
x: Overview # South-western Pacific. Geography # Bounded by Australia and New Zealand. Seafloor and geology # Deep (~5,943 m), with the Lord Howe Rise and seamount chains. Water and currents # The East Australian Current pushes warm water south. Climate, weather and cyclones # The East Australian Current is warming it rapidly, making it a marine heatwave hotspot. Flora and fauna # Range shifts of tropical species southward. Ecosystems # Lord Howe Island’s southernmost coral reef, kelp forests, and grey nurse sharks. History and exploration # Named after Abel Tasman (1642). People and economy # Fisheries. Threats and protection # Frequent marine heatwaves. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasman_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Tasman%20Sea

d: A huge inland sea where polar bears depend on seasonal ice.
x: Overview # In north-eastern Canada. Geography # Linked to the Arctic and Atlantic. Seafloor and geology # A shallow inland sea (average ~100 m) still rising after the ice age (~1 cm a year). Water and currents # Ice-covered for most of the year. Climate, weather and cyclones # Ice-covered most of the year; ice-free seasons lengthening, stressing polar bears. Flora and fauna # Polar bears, belugas. Ecosystems # Polar bears around Churchill, beluga whales in summer estuaries, and ringed seals. History and exploration # Henry Hudson’s 1610–11 expedition; the Hudson’s Bay Company fur trade. People and economy # Indigenous communities. Threats and protection # A shortening ice season. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Hudson%20Bay

d: The Arctic's 'hot spot' of warming, where Atlantic water is pushing north.
x: Overview # North of Norway and Russia. Geography # Arctic shelf sea. Seafloor and geology # A broad shelf sea (average ~230 m) warmed by Atlantic water. Water and currents # ‘Atlantification’ as warm Atlantic water reduces sea ice. Climate, weather and cyclones # Rapid ‘Atlantification’: sea ice retreating and Atlantic species moving in. Flora and fauna # The world’s largest cod stock, king crab (introduced). Ecosystems # Among the largest cod stocks, capelin, and introduced red king crabs. History and exploration # Willem Barentsz explored it in 1596; it was a WWII Arctic convoy route. People and economy # Major fisheries, oil and gas. Threats and protection # Rapid warming. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barents_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Barents%20Sea

d: The largest enclosed inland body of water, salty but not connected to the ocean.
x: Overview # A remnant of the ancient Paratethys Sea. Geography # Between Europe and Asia. Seafloor and geology # The largest enclosed inland body of water, in a basin below sea level; its deepest point is ~1,025 m. Water and currents # Brackish. Its level is falling. Climate, weather and cyclones # Water level fluctuates with Volga inflow and is now falling due to evaporation and warming. Flora and fauna # Beluga sturgeon (source of caviar), Caspian seals. Ecosystems # Beluga sturgeon and Caspian seals. History and exploration # Major oil and gas region since the 19th century. People and economy # Oil and gas. Threats and protection # Falling water levels, sturgeon decline. Sources # Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspian_Sea Marine Regions: https://www.marineregions.org/gazetteer.php?p=search&name=Caspian%20Sea

d: A tropical sea between Myanmar, Thailand and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
x: Overview # Lies east of the Andaman and Nicobar chain on an active back-arc basin. Geography # Bounded by Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia, Sumatra and India’s Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Seafloor and geology # Back-arc spreading centre with India’s only active volcano at Barren Island. Water and currents # Monsoon-driven circulation and large internal waves visible from space. Climate, weather and cyclones # Hit by the 2004 tsunami; cyclones form in spring and autumn. Flora and fauna # Coral reefs, dugongs, whale sharks and Moken sea nomads’ fishing grounds. Ecosystems # Reefs, mangroves, seagrass. History and exploration # Indian Ocean trade between India and Southeast Asia. People and economy # Tourism (Phuket, Havelock), fisheries.
